 Abstract

Objectives: This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of a systems-based secondary injury prevention

intervention aimed at early detection and management of hamstring strain injury (HSI) and time-loss

groin injury in an Australian male professional football club.

Design: Prospective cohort study.

Setting: Australian male professional football club.

Participants: Data were collected from male professional football players (n=73) from a single football

club.


                                                             oo
Main Outcome Measures: Unilateral knee flexion and side-lying hip adduction maximum voluntary

                                                               f
isometric contractions were monitored routinely in-season, two days post-match (≥40 hours [h]) during


                                                re
a three-season intervention period. Strength reductions greater than the tests’ minimal detectable change

                                                   -p
percentage prompted intervention. HSI and time-loss groin injury burdens were calculated per 1000
                                                      r
player hours and compared with those from an immediately preceding two-season control period, to

                                    lP
assess the effectiveness of the intervention.



                     ur
Results: Across the intervention period, there was a decrease in HSI (4.98 days absence/1000h (19.8%)


                       na
decrease) and time-loss groin injury burdens (0.57 days absence/1000h (49.1%) decrease) when

compared with the control period.

            Jo
Conclusions: A systems-based secondary injury prevention intervention shows preliminary positive

findings in reducing HSI and time-loss groin injury burdens within a male professional football club,

compared with usual care only.

Keywords: Sports medicine; screening; injury surveillance; team sport; soccer




                                                                                                       1
 Introduction

Hamstring strain injury (HSI) and time-loss groin injuries are common injuries in Australian male

professional football, accounting for between 12% to 22% and 8% to 18% of match-loss injuries,

respectively.1 In male professional football HSI incidence and burden rates have increased annually

between 2001 and 2014,2 while time-loss groin injury burden has remained consistent over a similar

period (2001 – 2016).3 Currently, evidence supporting the effectiveness of primary prevention exercise

programs in preventing muscle injury in elite football players is limited, with a deterioration of

compliance over the season shown previously in football studies.4,5 As primary prevention exercise


                                                             oo
programs alone have not been shown to significantly reduce these injuries,4,5 a complementary systems-

                                                               f
based approach, incorporating usual primary and tertiary injury prevention care alongside suitable


                                             re
secondary injury prevention for the early detection and management of HSI and time-loss groin injuries

may be more appropriate.6,7                     -p r
                                    lP
Secondary injury prevention involves screening for subclinical signs or symptoms in the period between

early detection through clinical screening and the usual time of diagnosis 8 following an exposure to a
                    urna
particular stressor (such as high intensity workloads in match-play football). It aims to allow early

intervention or treatment to prevent progression or worsening of the injury.9 Isometric strength

            Jo
reductions may precede the onset of HSI,10 while uninjured male professional football players

demonstrate stable hip strength capacity in-season.11 Regular monitoring of in-season isometric strength

may therefore form the basis of secondary injury prevention as part of a wider complementary systems-

based approach.



Football match-play can cause muscle damage and incite acute inflammatory responses12 and strength

deficits,13 all of which may inform the clinical reasoning and injury risk management process. Unilateral

knee flexion maximum voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) peak force is significantly reduced

immediately and 24 hours (h) post-match before returning to pre-match levels 48 h post-match in elite

youth footballers.13 Lingering strength deficits following this period may indicate incomplete recovery

that should be considered for follow-up by sports medicine staff before exposure to further workloads.

                                                                                                       2
 Previous research investigating the value of a systems-based approach, whereby usual primary and

tertiary injury prevention care is complemented with secondary injury prevention, shows promise in

reducing HSI incidence and burden6 and hip and groin injury burden.7 In this research HSI and groin

injury burden were able to be reduced via a strength screening alert and early indicated intervention

system in male youth football,6,7 however the feasibility and effectiveness of secondary injury

prevention of HSI and time-loss groin injuries in male professional football over multiple seasons, is

unknown.




                                                            oo
The purpose of this study was to assess the effectiveness of a systems-based secondary injury prevention

                                                              f
intervention for the early detection and management of HSI and time-loss groin injuries in an Australian


                                            re
male professional football club. It was hypothesised secondary injury prevention coupled with usual

                                               -p
primary and tertiary injury prevention care would reduce HSI and time-loss groin injury burdens.
                                                  r
Methods                            lP
                    ur
Study design and procedure


                      na
We conducted a prospective cohort study over five seasons in a cohort of professional football players.

The first two seasons served as the control period (2016/17 and 2017/18 seasons), while the following

            Jo
three seasons served as the intervention period (2018/19, 2019/20 and 2020/21 seasons). Data were

collected from male football players (n = 73) from a single football club. All players from the men’s

team were included in the study with players joining or leaving the team mid-season followed for their

respective periods. As such, the number of players varied over the five-season study period (21 in

2016/17, 25 in 2017/18, 28 in 2018/19, 29 in 2019/20 and 31 in 2020/21). Similarly due to the

longitudinal study design, there were four head coach, two physiotherapist and two strength and

conditioning coach changes across our five-season monitoring period. Ethical approval for the research

was obtained (protocol number H-2018-0229) and all players provided informed consent to participate

in the study.




                                                                                                      3
 For the first three seasons of this prospective cohort study (2016/17 – 2018/19), pre-season began in

July with the in-season commencing in October and ending in May. However, the COVID-19 pandemic

meant there was a three-month league-wide postponement of all football-related activities from March

to June in season 2019/20. Similarly, schedule changes arising from the pandemic meant a shortened

pre-season for the 2020/21 season, with pre-season beginning in October and in-season in December.



Control period methodology

Usual care was provided to players in the control period in the form of primary and tertiary injury


                                                              oo
prevention. Players underwent fatigue monitoring testing in the morning prior to every field training

                                                                f
session to ascertain training status, namely hip adduction strength and hamstring flexibility testing.


                                             re
These tests were not classified as part of a secondary injury prevention program due to a lack of test

                                                -p
sensitivity in detecting subclinical injury and were merely used as fatigue monitoring measures. Hip
                                                   r
adduction strength was assessed bilaterally with a standard commercially available aneroid

                                    lP
sphygmomanometer (Cumper and Robbins, Australia Medical Diagnostic Equipment Supplier) via the



                     ur
adductor squeeze test in short and long-lever test positions. For short-lever assessment the device was


                       na
placed between the knees while in a supine position with 45o of hip flexion, while for long-lever

assessment the device was placed between the medial malleoli while in a supine position with 0o of hip

            Jo
flexion and the feet placed flat on the floor.14 Strength was measured via pressure exerted (in millimetres

of mercury (mmHg)) with the sphygmomanometer recognised as a reliable and valid assessment of

isometric hip strength in athletic populations.15,16 Hamstring flexibility was assessed via the sit-and-

reach test with the result quantified in centimetres (cm). The sit-and-reach test is a reliable and valid

method of assessing hamstring flexibility and its protocol has been described previously.17 A

discrepancy of greater than one standard deviation from the player’s seasonal mean was used as an alert

for further assessment with the resultant procedure outlined in Supplementary Table 1. Management of

player training status was assessed by the team strength and conditioning coach, physiotherapist, and

sport scientist on a case-by-case basis. Indicated interventions to field training sessions were

proportionally based in response to player presentations to daily fatigue screening outlined above, as

well as subjective well-being questionnaire and workload data. These included the reduction or removal

                                                                                                         4
 of participation in drills containing high-speed running exposure, high-intensity acceleration and

deceleration and crossing.



Intervention period methodology

Usual care was provided to players in the intervention period in the form of primary and tertiary injury

prevention. In addition to usual care, a secondary injury prevention system was incorporated for the

early detection of subclinical signs or symptoms. Testing was administered in the morning prior to the

first training session of the week (two days post-match (MD+2) and following a rest day (≥40 h)).


                                                                 oo
Players were tested for unilateral knee flexion (prone, 45o hip flexion and 30o knee flexion) and side-

                                                                   f
lying hip adduction MVIC peak force (in Newtons [N]) using an externally fixed dynamometer


                                                re
(Applied Measurement Australia Pty Ltd, Melbourne, Australia). Isometric knee flexion testing was

                                                   -p
performed in accordance with previously published research to capture unilateral MVIC peak force,
                                                      r
whereby players exerted a five second MVIC against a dynamometer externally fixed to the floor

                                      lP
directly underneath the physiotherapy plinth.18 A side-lying unilateral isometric hip adduction testing

protocol was also integrated.19 Intra-rater reliability of the protocols was investigated via 29 uninjured
                      urna
players of the intervention period based on a single-measurement, absolute-agreement, two-way mixed-

effects model. Calculations indicated this sample size was sufficient, based on minimal acceptable

             Jo
reliability ρ0 = 0.7, expected reliability ρ1 = 0.9, α = 0.05 and β = 0.20.20 Intraclass correlation coefficient

(ICC3,1) estimates for isometric knee flexion and hip adduction were 0.83 – 0.90 and 0.66 – 0.76,

respectively, with minimal detectable change percentages (MDC%) 19.02% – 23% and 32.98% – 34%,

respectively.



An alert was created if a player had isometric knee flexion and/or hip adduction strength reductions

exceeding those of the respective test’s MDC values, when compared with the players’ 8-point moving

average (most recent 8 tests). Up to four alerts per player per testing session could be triggered from

each respective test and limb combination (left and right-sided unilateral knee flexion and hip

adduction). As MD+2 training sessions were very short in duration (< 45 minutes) and prescribed at

low intensities to facilitate recovery from the recent match, any alert generated on MD+2 did not affect

                                                                                                              5
 a player’s inclusion in this session unless otherwise agreed upon with medical staff. Re-testing then

occurred in the morning prior to training on MD+3, providing an additional 24 hours for the player to

recover from the reduction in strength. Only when strength deficits were still not restored on MD+3 in

comparison to their 8-point moving average did they then progress to the remaining stages of the

secondary injury prevention system (as per Figure 1). Where indicated, and following clinical

examination, subsequent interventions included daily physiotherapy treatment, inclusive of manual

therapy, prior to field training sessions for the remainder of the training week. Individualised muscle

activation, and strength programs were also to be completed before field sessions. These consisted


                                                             oo
primarily of the Copenhagen adduction exercise, isometric adduction, eccentric adduction sliders,

                                                               f
banded single- and double-leg bridging, lateral band walks, hop/jump landing practice and balance tasks


                                             re
on uneven surfaces with/without volleys (Supplementary Table 2). Load management during field

                                                -p
sessions focussed on a reduction in risk exposures, namely high-speed running efforts and distance,
                                                   r
explosive change of direction, and repetitive crossing and shooting actions.21 A shift to an on-field

                                    lP
playing position during training which inherently requires execution of less high-intensity activities,

such as a shift from wide to central positions,22 a reduction in the number of involvements in repetition-
                    urna
based drills, or a complete removal from the drill were specific indicated interventions. Consultative

decision-making between the sports medicine staff and head coach within the context of the planned

            Jo
training session was key across the intervention period. Post-training recovery modalities were

encouraged, inclusive of hydrotherapy and/or ice bath immersion.




                                                                                                        6
                                                        oof
                                           re -p r
                                  lP
                   urna
            Jo
Figure 1 (online version): Secondary injury prevention system for HSI and time-loss groin

injuries (adapted from Wollin et al 6,7)




                                                                                            7

Figure 1 (print version): Secondary injury prevention system for HSI and time-loss groin

injuries (adapted from Wollin et al 6,7)




                                                                                           8
 Player workload management

Player workload was individually monitored throughout the season by the team strength and

conditioning coach and sport scientist, with a standardised monitoring protocol utilised across both

reporting periods. All monitoring data were recorded using password protected athlete monitoring

software (Athlete Monitoring, Moncton, Canada), with player training status reviewed daily across both

reporting periods. Workload was quantified using both internal and external load measures and was

collected for all field and strength training sessions (inclusive of recovery/rehabilitation sessions) and

match-play (friendly and competitive). Global positioning system (GPS) data was used to quantify


                                                             oo
external load measures across all field sessions with monitored variables including total distance, and

                                                               f
distances covered at specific thresholds, namely high-speed distance (>19.8 km.h-1), and sprinting


                                             re
distance (>25.2 km.h-1). Internal load was collected across all sessions and was quantified by the session

                                                -p
rating of perceived exertion (sRPE) method23 which has been validated in football.24 In addition, players
                                                   r
across both reporting periods completed a club-tailored daily subjective well-being questionnaire

                                    lP
assessing sleep quality, muscle soreness and fatigue every morning to better inform training status. In-



                    ur
season, match-play typically occurred once per week occurring on a Friday, Saturday, or Sunday.


                      na
Injury definition and data collection

            Jo
An injury was defined as any physical complaint resulting from a football match or training leading to

the player being unable to fully participate in future matches or training (time-loss definition).25 As

such, both acute and longstanding groin injuries were encompassed within this definition. All injury

assessments were performed by the team physiotherapist and/or sports physician and a player was

considered injured until they were cleared to be available for match selection. Injuries were categorised

by severity and classified as being either: minimal (1 - 3 days absence from training and/or match-play),

mild (4 – 7 days absence), moderate (8 – 28 days absence) or severe (greater than 28 days absence).26

The surveillance period for the study included both the pre-season and in-season, inclusive of all

matches and training sessions. If a player was injured at the end of the season, a return-to-play date was

estimated based on all available evidence.25 All data collection protocols and data reporting adhered to



                                                                                                        9
 the consensus statement on injury definitions and data collection procedures in studies of football

injuries.25



Statistical analysis

Normality of the data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and visually via Q-Q plots. Welch’s t-

test for independent samples, equal variances not assumed, was used for parametric data (age, height,

and mass), while Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-parametric data (weekly training sessions,

weekly matches) to investigate differences between the control and intervention periods.27 Effect sizes


                                                            oo
were calculated using Hedges g for parametric data and the rank-biserial correlation r for non-

parametric data.27                                            f
                                            re -p
Poisson regression was used to analyse injury incidence rates (IIRs) with the number of observed
                                                  r
injuries as the response variable, cohort period as an independent variable and exposure as an offset. A

                                   lP
dispersion test from the ‘AER’ package28 was used to test the null hypothesis of equidispersion of the

response variable.29 A quasi-Poisson or negative binomial regression model was used instead where the
                       urna
assumption of equidispersion was not met. The potential confounding effects of age, height, and mass

on the response variable was also explored. Overall, match and training IIRs are reported as the number

              Jo
of injuries per 1000 player hours ((∑ injuries/ ∑ exposure hours) x 1000). Injury burden is reported

as days absence per 1000 player hours (injury incidence x mean severity). IIRs and rate ratios (RRs)

are reported with corresponding 95% CI, with intervals that did not include 1.0 indicating statistical

significance. All analyses were conducted using the statistical software R (Version 4.1.0).30



Results

A comparison of the control and intervention periods, inclusive of HSI and time-loss groin IIRs and

burdens, is shown in Table 1, while an injury burden matrix for HSI and time-loss groin injury is

presented in Figure 2. There were no significant differences in the age (p = 0.694), height (p = 0.818),

mass (p = 0.613), weekly training sessions (p = 0.162) or weekly matches (p = 0.304) between the

intervention and control periods. Overall, there were 10 HSI (6 dominant and 4 non-dominant) and 9

                                                                                                     10
 time-loss groin injuries (6 dominant and 3 non-dominant) in the control group, while there were 18 HSI

(5 dominant and 13 non-dominant) and 8 time-loss groin injuries (3 dominant and 5 non-dominant) in

the intervention group. No adverse events or injuries occurred as a result of strength testing in either

the control or intervention periods.



Hamstring Strain Injury

There was a 4.98 days absence/1000 h (19.8%) decrease in HSI burden (intervention period: 20.20 days

absence/1000 h; control period: 25.18 days absence/1000 h) in the intervention period compared with


                                                               oo
the control period. This was largely facilitated via the match-play related burden of HSI more than

                                                                 f
halving from the control period to the intervention period (48.46 days absence/1000 h (59.0%)


                                              re
decrease). The HSI incidence rates of the control and intervention periods were similar (RR: 1.04; 95%

                                                 -p
CI [0.49, 2.33]; p = 0.93) (Table 1); however, the severity of HSI was greater in the control period (20
                                                    r
± 11 days lost/HSI) compared to the intervention period (15 ± 8 days lost/HSI), although this was not

statistically significant (p = 0.265).   lP
                     ur
Time-Loss Groin Injury
                       na
There was a 3.93 days absence/1000 h (25.6%) reduction in time-loss groin injury burden (intervention

             Jo
period: 11.44 days absence/1000 h; control period: 15.37 days absence/1000 h) in the intervention

period compared with the control period. This was most pronounced in the burden resulting from match-

play, with an 18.26 days absence/1000 h (46.7%) decrease in the intervention period compared to the

control period. There was a 49% decrease in the incidence of time-loss groin injuries in the intervention

period (IIR: 0.59 injuries/1000 h; 95% CI [0.27, 1.11]) compared with that of the control period (IIR:

1.16 injuries/1000 h; 95% CI [0.56, 2.10]), however this did not reach statistical significance (RR: 0.51;

95% CI [0.19, 1.34]; p = 0.17). Time-loss groin injuries were more severe in the intervention period

however (19 ± 8 days lost/time-loss groin injury), compared to the control group (13 ± 8 days lost/time-

loss groin injury), although this was not statistically significant (p = 0.167).




                                                                                                       11
 Alerts

During the intervention period (2018/19 – 2020/21 seasons), there were 30 isometric strength reduction

alerts relating to 17 players (33% of the intervention period). Nine arose from right-sided knee flexion

(30%), seven from left-sided knee flexion (23%), ten from right-sided hip adduction (33%) and four

from left-sided hip adduction (13%) tests. Dominant limbs (57%) were more commonly affected than

non-dominant limbs (43%), while forwards (36.5%) were the position most prone to alerts, followed by

wide midfielders (20%), wide defenders (13.5%), central defenders (13.5%), goalkeepers (10%) and

central midfielders (6.5%).

                                                                                                              14
 Discussion

The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of a secondary injury prevention intervention in a

systems-based approach for the early detection and management of HSI and time-loss groin injuries

within an Australian male professional football club. A key finding of this study was that HSI and time-

loss groin injury burdens were reduced during the intervention period when compared with the control

period. Following the detection of subclinical forms of injury via greater screening and monitoring

practices, a cascade of indicated interventions shows preliminary positive evidence in reducing the

severity of HSI, albeit non-significantly. Forwards and wide positions within the intervention period


                                                             oo
were more prone to post-match isometric strength reduction alerts compared with central positions. This

                                                               f
highlights the potential for individual and position-based modifications to subsequent training sessions


                                             re
in the post-match period as part of a secondary injury prevention system.

                                                -p r
Adhering to the system parameters outlined in Figure 1, a reduction in the burdens of both HSI and

                                    lP
time-loss groin injury in male professional football players was observed, replicating results in the

literature of similar methodology.6 A notable difference between our current study and the previous
                    urna
study is the level of competition and the instability of coaching staff during these periods. Previously,

a novel HSI prevention system incorporating secondary prevention in addition to usual care (primary

             Jo
and tertiary prevention) was able to lower HSI burden in youth football players (12.9 days absence/1000

h (90.8%) decrease) when compared to usual care only (intervention period: 1.3 days absence/1000 h;

control period: 14.2 days absence/1000 h).6 While similarly, an early detection and management

strategy for the monitoring of hip and groin strength was able to reduce in-season hip and groin injury

burden when compared to pre-season (mean difference: -5.97 days absence; 95% CI [-11.27, -0.66]).7

It must be noted both studies were completed in youth football thus limiting the applicability to our

current study. Nevertheless, the implementation of early detection and indicated interventions alongside

primary and tertiary injury prevention shows promise in reducing HSI and time-loss groin injury

burdens.




                                                                                                      15
 We identified post-match isometric strength reduction trends which may be of value for practitioners in

the context of post-match monitoring and subsequent training prescription. Dominant limbs in our study

were more likely to have strength reductions than non-dominant limbs during testing two days post-

match (≥40 h). This is consistent with previous research in which post-match non-dominant isometric

hamstring strength (90o knee flexion) recovers quicker than that of dominant, with suggested links to a

higher frequency of technical actions (long passes and shots) performed using the dominant limb.31 We

also observed over a third of all strength reduction alerts to involve ‘forwards’, while wide positions

(wide midfielders and wide defenders) were more prone to alerts than central positions (central


                                                             oo
defenders and central midfielders). This may be attributed to forward and wide positions completing a

                                                               f
greater number of sprints and total sprint distance (p < 0.001) during match-play compared with central


                                             re
positions.22 Together these findings provide practitioners with relevant information to inform individual

                                                -p
and position-based modifications to subsequent training sessions in the post-match period as part of a

secondary injury prevention system.                r
                                    lP
                    ur
While the results of the present study suggest the introduction of secondary injury prevention within


                      na
male professional football may be useful to clubs, we refrain from advocating their use in isolation.

Recent study has shown repeated strength testing as a means of monitoring has limited predictive value

            Jo
for HSI,32 while there is limited evidence to support primary prevention exercise-based strategies alone

in preventing muscle injury in elite football.5 Instead, complementing the various pathology-based

(primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention) and risk factor-based (universal, selective and indicated)

injury prevention categorisations via an integrated systems-based approach is recommended.6,7,33

Despite these recommendations, there was no statistically significant evidence to suggest the daily

bilateral hip adductor squeeze peak force and hamstring (sit-and-reach) flexibility testing in the control

period failed to provide valuable insights to assist in reducing injury burden when compared to in-

season post-match testing within a secondary prevention systems-based approach.



A strength of this study is that it was undertaken within a male professional football club over multiple

seasons. The real-world application of the utilised injury prevention framework suggests its

                                                                                                       16
 implementation elsewhere is realistic and feasible. The test protocols are quick to administer, acceptable

to players and coaching staff and may be implemented in-season without interference to team schedules

or causing injury. Interventions are individualised and may be particularly pertinent during congested

match schedules. However, there are limitations to be noted within this study. We saw an increase,

albeit not statistically significant, in HSI incidence in the intervention period compared with the control

period. This increase in incidence may be due to a concept termed the ‘lead time problem’ where the

practice of increased screening and monitoring practices leads to a greater number of cases being

identified.8 Despite this increase in incidence, the early identification of injuries enabled the expedited


                                                              oo
application of indicated interventions to reduce injury severity and burden and to subsequently increase

                                                                f
player availability, which is linked to positive performance outcomes in football.34


                                              re -p
Due to the nature of professional sport, staffing changes across the study period were inevitable. There
                                                    r
were four head coach, two physiotherapist and two strength and conditioning coach changes across our

                                     lP
five-season study period. Due to this instability, internal relationships and communication quality



                     ur
between the coaching staff may have been affected. This is particularly relevant given high


                       na
communication quality between the medical team and head coach is associated with low injury burden,

low incidence of severe injuries, high training attendance and high match availability.35 Similarly,

            Jo
different coaching leadership styles have been proven to affect injury rates and player availability, with

a negative correlation between the overall level of transformational leadership of the head coach and

the incidence of severe injuries.36 While attributing causation is beyond the scope of our study, the effect

of coaching and medical staff instability is unknown, yet is likely to have contributed to the difference

in the outcome during periods of transition.35,36 As staffing changes are frequent in professional football,

this further supports the need for solid monitoring systems to help mitigate the influence of changing

staff profiles on player injury incidence and burden rates.



Results must also be considered with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in mind. There was an

increase in training injury burdens for HSI and time-loss groin injuries during the intervention period

(encompassing the restart to the 2019/2020 season following a three-month cessation of all team-based

                                                                                                         17
 activity due to COVID-19) compared with the control period. Recent research supports this trend, with

spikes identified in training injury burdens37 with links to short-term detraining effects due to

quarantine/periods of inactivity.38 Similarly, due to season schedule changes stemming from COVID-

19, there was a reduced pre-season for the 2020/21 season, with 65 days available for pre-season

training compared with a mean of 109 days from the preceding four seasons. This is particularly

pertinent given an increase of 10 pre-season sessions is linked with a decrease in severe injury incidence

(-0.20 severe injuries/1000 h) and injury burden (-21.8 layoff days/1000 h).39 Despite an increase in

training injury burdens linked to the COVID-19 pandemic, overall HSI and time-loss groin injury


                                                              oo
burdens were still reduced in the intervention period when compared with the control period.

                                                                f
                                              re
Finally, a non-randomised study design reduces the strength of the results obtained in the present study,

                                                 -p
which must be considered when interpreting the practical implications of this research. Despite a five-
                                                    r
season monitoring period, the relative strength of the study was also restricted by a sample size limited

                                     lP
to 21 – 31 players per season pertaining to one club only. The ability to generalise results outside of this



                     ur
specific context is therefore limited. A risk of confirmation bias may also have been present within this


                       na
study. Given the distinction between end of time loss and return to play is not objectively clear, 40 the

possibility of sports medicine staff subconsciously influencing return to play decision making of injured

             Jo
players to improve the effectiveness of the intervention must also be considered.



Conclusion

The implementation of a systems-based secondary injury prevention intervention provides preliminary

positive findings in reducing HSI and time-loss groin injury burdens in a cohort of male professional

football players, when compared with a control period. This study provides practitioners with a practical

framework that can be applied in male professional football, that is acceptable to players and coaches,

without interfering with normal team schedules.

Patients with TSK-11 of 17 or more (n = 19) more often had low Marx activity (73.7% vs 42.9%), hop limb symmetry index of 95% or less (55.6% vs 15%) and quadriceps LSI of 90% or less (50% vs 14.3%) than low-fear patients. 36	  "abstract": "Prospective cohort pilot of 40 patients cleared to return to sport after ACL reconstruction. 20	                                    Background: Outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) are highly variable. Previous studies have
21	                                    failed to report the relationship between fear, objective measures of function, and reinjury rates. The purpose of this study
22	                                    was to determine whether fear was related to functional performance measures and risk of second ACL injury after ACLR
23	                                    and return to sport (RTS).
24	                                    Hypothesis: Fear will be associated with performance on functional testing and second ACL injury rate.
25	                                    Study Design: Prospective cohort study.
26	                                    Level of Evidence: Level 2.
27	                                    Methods: A total of 40 patients cleared to RTS after ACLR completed the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-11), hop
28	                                    testing, and quadriceps strength testing, bilaterally. Patients were tracked for 12 months after RTS to identify the incidence of
29	                                    second ACL injury. Chi-square analyses determined whether patients with high fear (TSK-11, ≥17) were more likely to have
30	                                    lower levels of activity, greater asymmetry on functional testing, and higher reinjury rates.

32	                                    likely to report lower levels of activity, 7 times (OR, 7.1; 95% CI, 1.5-33.0) more likely to have a hop limb symmetry lower
33	                                    than 95%, and 6 times (OR, 6.0; 95% CI, 1.3-27.8) more likely to have quadriceps strength symmetry lower than

35	                                    19.8 ± 4.0) than those who did not suffer a second ACL injury (mean, 16.4 ± 3.6) (P = 0.03). Patients with a TSK-11 score of
36	                                    19 or greater at the time of RTS were 13 times (relative risk, 13.0; 95% CI, 2.1-81.0) more likely to suffer a second ACL tear

39	                                    isometric quadriceps strength, and had an increased risk of suffering a second ACL injury in the 24 months after RTS.

                                    Self-Reported Fear Predicts Functional
                                    Performance and Second ACL Injury
                                    After ACL Reconstruction and Return
                                    to Sport: A Pilot Study
                                    Mark V. Paterno, PT, PhD, MBA, SCS,*† Kaitlyn Flynn, DPT, SCS,‡ Staci Thomas, MS,§
                                    and Laura C. Schmitt, PT, PhD||

                                    Background: Outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) are highly variable. Previous studies have
                                    failed to report the relationship between fear, objective measures of function, and reinjury rates. The purpose of this study
                                    was to determine whether fear was related to functional performance measures and risk of second ACL injury after ACLR
                                    and return to sport (RTS).
                                    Hypothesis: Fear will be associated with performance on functional testing and second ACL injury rate.
                                    Study Design: Prospective cohort study.
                                    Level of Evidence: Level 2.
                                    Methods: A total of 40 patients cleared to RTS after ACLR completed the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-11), hop
                                    testing, and quadriceps strength testing, bilaterally. Patients were tracked for 12 months after RTS to identify the incidence of
                                    second ACL injury. Chi-square analyses determined whether patients with high fear (TSK-11, ≥17) were more likely to have
                                    lower levels of activity, greater asymmetry on functional testing, and higher reinjury rates.
                                    Results: Patients with greater fear on the TSK-11 (≥17) at RTS were 4 times (odds ratio [OR], 3.73; 95% CI, 0.98-14.23) more
                                    likely to report lower levels of activity, 7 times (OR, 7.1; 95% CI, 1.5-33.0) more likely to have a hop limb symmetry lower
                                    than 95%, and 6 times (OR, 6.0; 95% CI, 1.3-27.8) more likely to have quadriceps strength symmetry lower than
                                    90%. Patients who went on to suffer an ipsilateral second ACL injury had a greater TSK-11 score at the time of RTS (mean,
                                    19.8 ± 4.0) than those who did not suffer a second ACL injury (mean, 16.4 ± 3.6) (P = 0.03). Patients with a TSK-11 score of
                                    19 or greater at the time of RTS were 13 times (relative risk, 13.0; 95% CI, 2.1-81.0) more likely to suffer a second ACL tear
                                    within 24 months after RTS.
                                    Conclusion: Patients with greater self-reported fear were less active, presented with lower single-leg hop performance and
                                    isometric quadriceps strength, and had an increased risk of suffering a second ACL injury in the 24 months after RTS.
                                    Clinical Relevance: Self-reported fear of movement/reinjury after ACLR at the time of RTS may be an important measure
                                    to incorporate into discharge criteria prior to release to return to pivoting and cutting sports after ACLR.
                                    Keywords: ACL reconstruction; second injury; fear; functional performance

40	31 Abstract
41	32 Background
42	33 The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) plays an important sensory role within the sensorimotor
43	34 system. Following ACL injury, sensorimotor dysfunction can have implications for rehabilitation and
44	35 risk of reinjury.
45	36 Clinical question
46	37 What dysfunction occurs within the sensorimotor system following ACL injury, and how can
47	38 clinicians assess it?
48	39 Key results
49	40 Following ACL injury, dysfunction occurs across the sensorimotor system: afferent pathways, efferent
50	41 pathways and central processing. The afferent pathways exhibit dysfunction within the
51	42 somatosensory system ([1] increased pain and swelling, [2] increased central cortical processing and
52	43 [3] reduced proprioception). There is also dysfunction in the visual system (increased visual-motor
53	44 reliance and central cortical processing). The efferent pathways have reduced excitability of the
54	45 central cortex, reduced descending motor pathway excitability and altered spinal reflexive excitability
55	46 (acutely reduced but then chronically increased).
56	47 Clinical application
57	48 Protocols to assess athletes’ sensorimotor function following ACL injury might help clinicians quantify
58	49 the risk of reinjury. Assessing central processing requires specialised equipment, not typically
59	50 accessible to clinicians. A practical approach to quantify the extent of sensorimotor dysfunction could
60	51 focus on assessing the afferent and efferent pathways: tests of proprioception (e.g. joint position
61	52 sense test), pain (e.g. visual analogue scale and numerical pain rating scale), swelling (e.g. sweep test
62	53 and ballottement test), visual-motor reliance (e.g. stepdown test), visual-motor processing ability (e.g.
63	54 sensory stations or neurocognitive tests), muscle strength (e.g. repetition maximum testing or
64	55 isokinetic dynamometry) and voluntary activation (e.g. electromyography).
65	56 Key words
66	57 Anterior cruciate ligament, sensorimotor dysfunction, assessment, rehabilitation, afferent, efferent
67	58 Introduction
68	59 The sensorimotor system is complex, and a central element of the body’s motor control system that
69	60 assists with planning and executing movement.82 It encompasses the afferent sensory systems, the
70	61 efferent motor pathways and the processing within the central cortex.82 The afferent sensory systems
71	62 include: visual, somatosensory (interpreting sensations from the skin and within the body such as pain,
72	63 touch and vibration), vestibular (balance and spatial orientation), olfactory, gustation and auditory
73	64 systems.55,76 Integrating sensory information from afferent systems, especially the somatosensory
74	65 and visual systems, allows the individual to gain accurate information from the environment to guide
75	66 an appropriate movement strategy (Figure 1). The efferent motor pathways then signal the muscles
76	67 to execute the desired movement strategy.
77	Figure 1. An individual uses somatosensory and visual systems to gather information that helps the
78	sensorimotor cortex create an appropriate motor response.
79	68 Musculoskeletal injuries, including anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries, lead to sensorimotor
80	69 system changes, and ultimately sensorimotor dysfunction.27,33,40,57,61 The dysfunction manifests as
81	70 errors in planning and executing movement.94 Sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL reconstruction
82	71 (ACLR) may be a risk factor in sustaining a new ACL injury,28,94 even after completing rehabilitation.
83	72 Therefore, clinicians must understand how sensorimotor dysfunction occurs following ACL injury, how
84	73 to assess it and rehabilitate it.
85	74 This clinical commentary outlines sensorimotor changes following an ACL injury, and proposes
86	75 evidence-based methods to identify dysfunction, that are driven by our clinical practice. In part 2, we
87	76 focus on rehabilitation techniques for sensorimotor dysfunction.
88	77 Clinical Question
89	78 What sensorimotor dysfunction occurs following ACL injury and how can clinicians assess it? The ACL
90	79 has two important roles: (1) providing structural knee stability by limiting excessive anterior
91	80 translation and internal rotation of the tibia, and knee valgus,11,89 and (2) providing sensory
92	81 information to the sensorimotor cortex to facilitate motor planning and execution.22,68 Even when
93	82 structural stability is restored after ACLR, sensorimotor dysfunction remains,24,27 which may impair
94	83 gathering sensorimotor information from the environment when planning movement. Alterations in
95	84 efferent motor pathways remain following ACLR, even up to two years post-surgery with reduced
96	85 strength and activation of the quadriceps.31,35
97	86 Clinicians may lack either the clinical tools to identify individuals with sensorimotor dysfunction, or
98	87 rehabilitation methods may be inadequate. Dysfunction in the sensorimotor system following ACLR is
99	88 the same as for ACL injuries that are managed non-operatively and therefore, the two conditions
100	89 (ACLR and ACL injuries) are not separated.
101	90 How does sensorimotor dysfunction impact movements?
102	91 Motor planning and execution is complex. Neurocognitive demands (processing sensory, motor,
103	92 emotional and higher executive information) are increased in sporting situations due to movement
104	93 speed, greater decision-making complexity and reduced decision-making time. An athlete’s
105	94 movement strategy is determined by their constraints (anthropometrics and neuromuscular
106	95 capacities), the perceived environment information (opposition position and movement) and task
107	96 constraints (e.g. attempting to score a goal).2,12,102 Perception of environmental information and action
108	97 continuously occurs,20 requiring the athlete to integrate sensory information to generate an
109	98 appropriate movement strategy. Individuals have several sensory systems: visual, somatosensory
110	99 (interpreting sensations from the skin and within the body such as pain, touch and vibration),
111	100 vestibular (balance and spatial orientation), olfactory (smell), gustation (taste) and auditory
112	101 (hearing),55,76 with the somatosensory and visual systems being the most pertinent for motor planning
113	102 and execution. Therefore, sensorimotor dysfunction can increase neurocognitive demands or reduce
114	103 the ability to plan high impact movements efficiently (such as cutting or jumping/landing).
115	104 Key results
116	105 Somatosensory system
117	106 The somatosensory system (1) informs the central cortex about the position and movement of body
118	107 segments (proprioception) and, (2) senses painful and pressure/vibration stimuli.76 Proprioception
119	108 uses fast velocity afferent fibres (within muscle, ligament and joint tissue) to provide starting posture
120	109 information so that appropriate coordination of motor units can be produced to execute a
121	110 movement.75 The second somatosensory function uses soft tissue pain and pressure receptors to
122	111 detect pain or swelling so that if an injury occurs or tissue damage is imminent, then the body can
123	112 coordinate a motor response to minimise damage or protect the injured structure.81,86
124	113 A full-thickness ACL tear results in a complete loss of mechanoreceptors.14 The return of these
125	114 mechanoreceptors following ACLR is often slow and variable,14 which may lead to altered
126	115 somatosensory processing and a reorganisation of the sensorimotor cortex with greater reliance being
127	116 placed on the visual system.57 Diminished proprioceptive ability following ACLR may mean greater
128	117 error for the athlete when determining how their body is positioned in the environment. Knee
129	118 proprioception is reduced after ACLR, compared to both the uninjured limb and healthy control limbs,
130	119 even after rehabilitation and return to sport.42,79,80 Changes in surgical technique to preserve the
131	120 remnants of the ACL during reconstructive surgery may improve proprioception,7 but the surgical
132	121 technique is uncommon.
133	122 Pain and swelling following an ACL injury may inhibit quadriceps activation.81 Knee joint effusion
134	123 causes activation of afferent pressure receptors within the joint capsule60 due to high intra-articular
135	124 pressures, and chemical activation of the receptors due to inflammatory cytokines.81 Afferent pressure
136	125 receptor activations may reduce quadriceps activity64 and strength. 53 Similarly, pain and inflammation
137	126 can sensitise afferent receptors within the joint capsule and connective tissues, leading to further
138	127 quadriceps inhibition,60,81 with strength losses of 80-90% within the first few days following knee
139	128 surgery, which may persist in the weeks after.87 It is therefore essential to measure and monitor
140	129 athlete pain and effusion throughout the rehabilitation process.
141	130 Assessment
142	131 Assessing somatosensory function involves assessing somatosensory cortical processing demands,
143	132 assessing proprioception, and assessing pain and effusion (Table 1). However, the former generally
144	133 uses equipment (e.g. functional brain MRI) not readily accessible. Therefore, clinicians should focus
145	134 on assessing proprioception, pain and effusion.
146	135 Proprioception
147	136 Examining proprioceptive function is difficult because it covers several domains: (1) joint position
148	137 sense, (2) sense of movement (kinaesthesia), (3) sense of movement velocity, and (4) sense of force.75
149	138 Methods to examine kinaesthesia, sense of velocity and sense of force use specialised tools, such as
150	139 isokinetic dynamometers. However, joint position sense (JPS) testing is more easily accessible and
151	140 demonstrates significant proprioceptive impairment in the ACLR limb21,80 and we recommend its use.

216	141
217	142 JPS testing can be split into three broad categories: image/photograph recorded angulation testing,
218	143 electrogoniometry, and isokinetic dynamometry. While all three approaches can be reliable,19,59,74,78
219	144 some protocols have poor reliability.90 Larger absolute errors between target angle and athlete’s
220	145 angle replication attempt indicate JPS deficit. An image-recorded angulation JPS testing method can
221	146 be easily implemented in the clinic and with good reliability (ICC=0.96-0.98) (Appendix A).77-79 Among
222	147 10 elites athletes with ACLR, there was a difference of 5.3° in absolute error between the ACLR limb
223	148 (absolute error= 7.2°) and the uninjured limb (absolute error= 1.9°), reflecting ACLR proprioceptive
224	149 dysfunction.79. We recommend JPS testing every four to six weeks during rehabilitation.
225	150 Assessing pain and effusion
226	151 Regularly assessing joint pain and effusion is essential to minimise potential muscle inhibition,
227	152 particularly in the quadriceps and hamstrings,54 and to ensure that the athlete’s knee is tolerating
228	153 rehabilitation program progressions. Numeric rating scale and visual analogue scale are valid and
229	154 reliable measures, so select a method based on what the athlete prefers.99 A minimal clinically
230	155 important change in numeric rating scale has not been examined in the ACLR population; it is 2 points
231	156 in people with chronic musculoskeletal pain.85 The visual analogue scale requires athletes to mark
232	157 their pain on a 10-centimetre line between ‘0’ (no pain) and ’10 centimetres’ (worst pain imaginable).
233	158 A minimal clinically important change of 1.4 centimetres is suggested for musculoskeletal conditions
234	159 and chronic pain.13,39 If pain persists, then consider strategies to manage pain, especially during early
235	160 stage rehabilitation as pain may inhibit muscle recruitment34 and result in limb off-loading strategies.
236	161 During mid-to-late stage rehabilitation, pain that negatively affects execution of sporting motor tasks
237	162 or rehabilitation exercises also needs addressing. Pain assessments should be completed every session
238	163 with the clinician until the pain resolves to assess how the athlete is responding to their interventions.
239	164 Measuring effusion following ACL injury is not a direct measure of afferent function but allows
240	165 clinicians to assess a secondary factor (pressure or inflammation) that may be inhibiting
241	166 mechanoreceptors within and surrounding the knee. The sweep test and the ballottement test
242	167 (Appendix B) both have good inter-observer agreement8. Effusion testing should be completed every
243	168 session the athlete has with the clinician until resolved to ensure that the knee is responding
244	169 appropriately.
245	170 Visual system
246	171 The visual system may be the predominant sensory system used when planning and executing motor
247	172 tasks.16,23,93 When there is conflict between somatosensory system and visual system afferent
248	173 information, the visual information takes precedence.70,93 The common thread through theories of
249	174 how visual information is processed is that the information from the visual system provides the central
250	175 cortex with information regarding what is in the environment and where it is positioned.16
251	176 There is limited research examining the changes that occur to the visual system and how visual
252	177 information is processed following ACL injury. The term visual-motor system encompasses all visual
253	178 processes and how they influence motor actions.4,23,24,26 Functional brain MRI studies show increased
254	179 activity in the visual processing cortices following ACLR.27,61 Increased visual processing activity may
255	180 stem from loss of proprioception during ACL injury and the subsequent effusion and nociception.24
256	181 Altered afferent information to the sensorimotor cortex leads to reduced postural control, and
257	182 increased demands on motor planning centres in the frontal lobe and secondary somatosensory
258	183 cortices (as evidenced by functional brain MRI).6,27,57 To manage reduced postural control and knee
259	184 afferent input, a re-weighting of the sensory systems may occur with an increased reliance placed on
260	185 visual information during motor planning and execution.27 This re-weighting potentially contributes to
261	186 increased cognitive demand which may be detrimental to an athlete by reducing their ability to react
262	187 quickly to their changing environment.6,37 Given the potential link between increased reliance on the
263	188 visual-motor system and ACLR reinjury,28 it is important that clinicians assess for potential increased
264	189 visual reliance.25
265	190 Assessment
266	191 Assessment of visual function commonly covers two domains: visual-motor processing ability and
267	192 increased reliance on the visual-motor system via balance tests (Table 2).
268	193 Visual-motor processing ability
269	194 This encompasses all processes that occur from an athlete using their eyes to capture environmental
270	195 information, the processing of the information in the central cortex and its influence on motor
271	196 execution.96,97 Poor visual-motor processing ability (visual memory, reaction time and processing
272	197 speed) may contribute to non-contact ACL injuries as assessed with the ImPACT computer-based
273	198 neurocognitive test (ImPACT Applications Inc.).95
274	199 Different companies (e.g. ImPACT [https://impacttest.com/], and Cogstate
275	200 [https://www.cogstate.com/]) provide computer-based neurocognitive tests that are easy for
276	201 clinicians to administer at a relatively low cost, even on a large scale. These tests are reliable in
277	202 uninjured athletes58 but no study has examined their reliability in the ACLR population. A common
278	203 issue with the neurocognitive tests is that they predominantly test memory and speed of processing
279	204 domains, with a lack of varied visual-motor domains.
280	205 ‘Sensory stations’ and tablet systems (e.g. Senaptec, Oregon USA) with visual-motor specific testing
281	206 make it easier to assess across a number of visual-motor domains that reflect visual acuity (discern
282	207 shapes and object details), visual memory (store visual information so that learning can occur from
283	208 previous experiences), near-far eye movements (switch gaze from near to far objects) and multiple
284	209 object tracking ability (pick up multiple environmental cues)
285	210 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4Vj78RX7oVo).
286	211 The sensory station has good reliability in uninjured athletes,17 but no studies have examined its
287	212 reliability in the ACLR population . While measures of visual-motor performance can predict in-game
288	213 performances in sports such as professional baseball,41,49 there is currently no research examining
289	214 ACL injury risk or changes in visual-motor function following injury . As such, there is limited
290	215 information on what a good baseline score is for each of the visual-motor domains. For the tests to
291	216 be beneficial, athlete baseline information is required to determine if function has been negatively
292	217 affected by injury. We have found athletes enjoy engaging in the sensory station due to the novelty
293	218 and the varied challenging tasks. Their results can be exported as raw scores so that deeper analysis
294	219 can be conducted. The athlete is provided with an immediate percentile score (against other
295	220 athletes from similar sports) which drives competition and engagement.

343	222 Assessing visual-motor reliance via balance tests
344	223 Balance tests are common in clinical settings to assess an athlete’s ability to integrate sensory
345	224 (somatosensory, visual and vestibular) information. The athlete performs a task that compares their
346	225 balance under two conditions: eyes open versus eyes closed. A greater deficit in performance, as
347	226 compared to either normative data or the uninjured limb, indicates an increased visual-motor system
348	227 reliance.
349	228 Postural control worsens when vision is obstructed during single-limb standing in ACL deficient
350	229 individuals as compared to healthy participants.103 However, the ACLR population exhibits similar
351	230 reductions in postural control performance as healthy participants (ACLR 43% reduction vs controls
352	231 45% reduction),103 suggesting that either: (1) visual-motor reliance does not negatively affect an ACLR
353	232 athlete’s ability to maintain postural control in comparison to healthy controls, or (2) the task of quasi-
354	233 static standing on one leg may not be challenging enough.
355	234 We adapted a 20cm stepdown task (Colby et al)9 in which athletes step onto a force plate where they
356	235 must attain stability as quickly as possible (Appendix C). Athletes complete this with eyes open and
357	236 then eyes closed, with time to stability used as the outcome measure.5,9 We found good reliability
358	237 (ICCs= 0.71-0.96) (unpublished) and a visual-motor reliance index score can be ascribed to athletes.
359	238 Our findings show that healthy athletes improved their time to stability time by 17% with eyes closed.
360	239 Therefore, if an athlete’s time to stability worsens with eyes closed, we attribute this to visual reliance
361	240 and suggest they would benefit from targeted rehabilitation strategies. If clinicians do not have access
362	241 to force plates, subjective assessment of postural control (assessing frontal plane control, trunk sway,
363	242 hip movement, knee adduction, and foot pronation and supination) may be used to assess athlete
364	243 performance. We reassess visual-motor reliance every six weeks.
365	244 Efferent system
366	245 The main efferent system components involved in motor planning and execution are the motor cortex,
367	246 descending motor pathway and spinal-reflexive pathways.73,104 After ACL injury, there are changes in
368	247 all three components,71 which are still evident 6 months following ACLR,44 manifesting in changes in
369	248 muscle activation, coordination56 and reduced muscle strength.43 This likely contributes (along with
370	249 muscle atrophy) to persistent quadriceps weakness65,73 and ongoing dysfunction.50,72 Following ACLR,
371	250 unilateral and bilateral deficits in quadriceps voluntary activation are present up to four years post-
372	251 surgery.48,71 Deficits in quadriceps activation can result in reduced strength and performance,51 and
373	252 increased risk of reinjury.69 Although there is some debate,71 the driver of the strength deficit is likely:
374	253 (1) alterations to the efferent system (motor cortex, descending motor pathway and spinal-reflexive
375	254 pathways), (2) local muscle atrophy, and (3) negative influences from changes in the sensory system
376	255 (as previously discussed).
377	256 Motor cortex
378	257 The motor cortex (e.g. premotor cortex and primary motor cortex) is involved in movement planning
379	258 and initiation.47 Following ACLR, there is increased intracortical inhibition associated with reduced
380	259 voluntary quadriceps activation in the injured limb,52 which can occur bilaterally.105 Subsequently, the
381	260 athlete needs to dedicate greater neural resources and effort to activate a muscle and execute
382	261 movement, compared to preinjury, thereby potentially resulting in non-optimal movement
383	262 strategies.6,25
384	263 Descending motor pathway
385	264 The descending motor pathway (corticospinal tract) carries impulses from the motor cortex through
386	265 the spinal cord to synapse with the lower motor neurone that activates the target muscle.38,84 Its
387	266 excitability is reduced following ACLR via an increased firing threshold44,71 which may occur in response
388	267 to increased motor cortex inhibition.29,44 The increased threshold results in reduced quadriceps
389	268 activation,71 which may change movement strategies.
390	269 Spinal Reflexive pathways and peripheral changes
391	270 Spinal reflexive pathways facilitate fast motor responses to peripheral stimuli. ACL injury and ACLR
392	271 lead to pain, knee joint effusion and loss of proprioceptors within the native ACL,66 which inhibits the
393	272 quadriceps and increases hamstrings motor activity..36,88 Over time, the excitability of the spinal
394	273 reflexive pathway to the quadriceps increases such that it is significantly greater in both the ACLR limb
395	274 and unreconstructed limb in comparison to healthy athletes.83,98
396	275 All components of the efferent system (motor cortex, descending motor pathway and spinal reflexive
397	276 pathways) are influenced by ACL injury. An initial reduction in excitability occurs within the spinal
398	277 reflexive pathways and motor cortex. Reductions in descending motor pathway volume and
399	278 excitability can then develop, with changes occurring 3-6 months post ACLR.45 These factors may
400	279 culminate in reduced voluntary activation and function of the quadriceps,71 negatively impacting
401	280 strength and knee control improvements during rehabilitation.
402	281 Assessment
403	282 Assessing the efferent subsystems is primarily conducted with specialised testing equipment and
404	283 expertise generally unavailable to clinicians. These include Hoffman reflex to assess spinal reflexive
405	284 changes, transcranial magnetic stimulation to determine corticospinal excitability, and central
406	285 activation ratio to measure voluntary activation levels of muscles.44 Therefore, clinicians should
407	286 measure muscle strength and activation (especially the quadriceps) to determine efferent function
408	287 following ACLR. These tests cannot differentiate which efferent system component is dysfunctional,
409	288 so management strategies should be generalised to improving overall efferent function (Table 3).

485	290 Quadriceps and hamstrings strength can be tested via repetition maximum testing (1, 3 or 5 repetition
486	291 maximum), handheld dynamometry or isokinetic dynamometry. Although they do not provide
487	292 equivalent measures,18 repetition maximum testing is best placed to examine strength changes
488	293 through a specific movement such as squats, knee extensions or deadlifts18 which may help clinicians
489	294 understand if the athlete’s functional patterns are improving. A limitation of using repetition
490	295 maximum strength testing is that multi-joint movements may improve due to improved inter-
491	296 segmental coordination, which may mask any lack of improvement in isolated quadriceps strength.
492	297 Isokinetic dynamometry is the gold standard for examining muscle strength (Appendix D).15,18 It has
493	298 high reliability (ICC= 0.74 – 0.93)30,91 when assessing quadriceps and hamstrings peak torque. Elite
494	299 male field-based athletes should be achieving a quadriceps and hamstrings peak torque of 3.19±0.1
495	300 Nm/kg and 1.78±0.1 Nm/kg; elite female field-based athletes should achieve values of 2.32±0.36
496	301 Nm/kg and 1.36±0.21Nm/kg.101 In our practice, athletes falling below these levels are prescribed
497	302 strategies to improve strength and efferent function. Although access to isokinetic dynamometry is
498	303 improving, it may still be out of reach for many clinicians. Handheld dynamometry is a cost-effective
499	304 alternative. It is reliable and valid in measuring isometric quadriceps strength when using non-elastic
500	305 straps.1,46 One disadvantage is that it cannot identify range-specific strength deficits.32 Strength
501	306 assessments should be completed every 6-8 weeks.
502	307 Deficits in quadriceps voluntary activation persist following ACLR.48 Surface EMG biofeedback devices
503	308 are accessible and can determine the magnitude of motor unit recruitment during a contraction,
504	309 which can give insight into any potential altered efferent function. Commercially available surface
505	310 EMG biofeedback units (e.g. ‘mTrigger’, LLC, Delaware, USA, and Neurotrac Myo Plus 2, Verity Medical
506	311 Ltd) have reported that they can compare EMG activity between limbs via dual-channel EMG. The
507	312 athlete performs 3-6 repetitions of maximal isometric quadriceps activation on the injured and
508	313 healthy limbs, with the surface electrodes placed over the motor points of the quadriceps. Differences
509	314 of more than 22%-30% may be clinically-relevant10,67 and can guide clinicians to implement
510	315 appropriate strategies to improve efferent function.3,92 We suggest assessing every 2 weeks until no
511	316 significant difference is noted (Appendix E).
512	317 Summary
513	318 Sensorimotor dysfunction may persist following ACL injury and occurs across all aspects of the
514	319 sensorimotor system: afferent pathways, efferent pathways and central processing (Figure 2). We
515	320 recommend clinicians focus on assessing the somatosensory, visual and efferent systems. Routine
516	321 assessment of the somatosensory system (JPS testing, pain and effusion testing) and visual system
517	322 (visual-motor reliance testing and visual-motor processing testing) will guide clinical decisions.
518	323 Assessing efferent function via strength testing and EMG assessment for voluntary activation can be
519	324 easily implemented into clinical practice.

522	326 Findings: Sensorimotor dysfunction can occur following an ACL injury. It occurs across the
523	327 somatosensory, visual and efferent systems.
524	328 Implications: All three systems should be assessed: somatosensory (JPS, pain and effusion tests),
525	329 visual system (visual-motor reliance and visual-motor processing tests), and efferent system
526	330 (strength and voluntary activation tests)
