31 Abstract
32 Background
33 The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) plays an important sensory role within the sensorimotor
34 system. Following ACL injury, sensorimotor dysfunction can have implications for rehabilitation and
35 risk of reinjury.
36 Clinical question
37 What dysfunction occurs within the sensorimotor system following ACL injury, and how can
38 clinicians assess it?
39 Key results
40 Following ACL injury, dysfunction occurs across the sensorimotor system: afferent pathways, efferent
41 pathways and central processing. The afferent pathways exhibit dysfunction within the
42 somatosensory system ([1] increased pain and swelling, [2] increased central cortical processing and
43 [3] reduced proprioception). There is also dysfunction in the visual system (increased visual-motor
44 reliance and central cortical processing). The efferent pathways have reduced excitability of the
45 central cortex, reduced descending motor pathway excitability and altered spinal reflexive excitability
46 (acutely reduced but then chronically increased).
47 Clinical application
48 Protocols to assess athletes’ sensorimotor function following ACL injury might help clinicians quantify
49 the risk of reinjury. Assessing central processing requires specialised equipment, not typically
50 accessible to clinicians. A practical approach to quantify the extent of sensorimotor dysfunction could
51 focus on assessing the afferent and efferent pathways: tests of proprioception (e.g. joint position
52 sense test), pain (e.g. visual analogue scale and numerical pain rating scale), swelling (e.g. sweep test
53 and ballottement test), visual-motor reliance (e.g. stepdown test), visual-motor processing ability (e.g.
54 sensory stations or neurocognitive tests), muscle strength (e.g. repetition maximum testing or
55 isokinetic dynamometry) and voluntary activation (e.g. electromyography).
56 Key words
57 Anterior cruciate ligament, sensorimotor dysfunction, assessment, rehabilitation, afferent, efferent
58 Introduction
59 The sensorimotor system is complex, and a central element of the body’s motor control system that
60 assists with planning and executing movement.82 It encompasses the afferent sensory systems, the
61 efferent motor pathways and the processing within the central cortex.82 The afferent sensory systems
62 include: visual, somatosensory (interpreting sensations from the skin and within the body such as pain,
63 touch and vibration), vestibular (balance and spatial orientation), olfactory, gustation and auditory
64 systems.55,76 Integrating sensory information from afferent systems, especially the somatosensory
65 and visual systems, allows the individual to gain accurate information from the environment to guide
66 an appropriate movement strategy (Figure 1). The efferent motor pathways then signal the muscles
67 to execute the desired movement strategy.
Figure 1. An individual uses somatosensory and visual systems to gather information that helps the
sensorimotor cortex create an appropriate motor response.
68 Musculoskeletal injuries, including anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries, lead to sensorimotor
69 system changes, and ultimately sensorimotor dysfunction.27,33,40,57,61 The dysfunction manifests as
70 errors in planning and executing movement.94 Sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL reconstruction
71 (ACLR) may be a risk factor in sustaining a new ACL injury,28,94 even after completing rehabilitation.
72 Therefore, clinicians must understand how sensorimotor dysfunction occurs following ACL injury, how
73 to assess it and rehabilitate it.
74 This clinical commentary outlines sensorimotor changes following an ACL injury, and proposes
75 evidence-based methods to identify dysfunction, that are driven by our clinical practice. In part 2, we
76 focus on rehabilitation techniques for sensorimotor dysfunction.
77 Clinical Question
78 What sensorimotor dysfunction occurs following ACL injury and how can clinicians assess it? The ACL
79 has two important roles: (1) providing structural knee stability by limiting excessive anterior
80 translation and internal rotation of the tibia, and knee valgus,11,89 and (2) providing sensory
81 information to the sensorimotor cortex to facilitate motor planning and execution.22,68 Even when
82 structural stability is restored after ACLR, sensorimotor dysfunction remains,24,27 which may impair
83 gathering sensorimotor information from the environment when planning movement. Alterations in
84 efferent motor pathways remain following ACLR, even up to two years post-surgery with reduced
85 strength and activation of the quadriceps.31,35
86 Clinicians may lack either the clinical tools to identify individuals with sensorimotor dysfunction, or
87 rehabilitation methods may be inadequate. Dysfunction in the sensorimotor system following ACLR is
88 the same as for ACL injuries that are managed non-operatively and therefore, the two conditions
89 (ACLR and ACL injuries) are not separated.
90 How does sensorimotor dysfunction impact movements?
91 Motor planning and execution is complex. Neurocognitive demands (processing sensory, motor,
92 emotional and higher executive information) are increased in sporting situations due to movement
93 speed, greater decision-making complexity and reduced decision-making time. An athlete’s
94 movement strategy is determined by their constraints (anthropometrics and neuromuscular
95 capacities), the perceived environment information (opposition position and movement) and task
96 constraints (e.g. attempting to score a goal).2,12,102 Perception of environmental information and action
97 continuously occurs,20 requiring the athlete to integrate sensory information to generate an
98 appropriate movement strategy. Individuals have several sensory systems: visual, somatosensory
99 (interpreting sensations from the skin and within the body such as pain, touch and vibration),
100 vestibular (balance and spatial orientation), olfactory (smell), gustation (taste) and auditory
101 (hearing),55,76 with the somatosensory and visual systems being the most pertinent for motor planning
102 and execution. Therefore, sensorimotor dysfunction can increase neurocognitive demands or reduce
103 the ability to plan high impact movements efficiently (such as cutting or jumping/landing).
104 Key results
105 Somatosensory system
106 The somatosensory system (1) informs the central cortex about the position and movement of body
107 segments (proprioception) and, (2) senses painful and pressure/vibration stimuli.76 Proprioception
108 uses fast velocity afferent fibres (within muscle, ligament and joint tissue) to provide starting posture
109 information so that appropriate coordination of motor units can be produced to execute a
110 movement.75 The second somatosensory function uses soft tissue pain and pressure receptors to
111 detect pain or swelling so that if an injury occurs or tissue damage is imminent, then the body can
112 coordinate a motor response to minimise damage or protect the injured structure.81,86
113 A full-thickness ACL tear results in a complete loss of mechanoreceptors.14 The return of these
114 mechanoreceptors following ACLR is often slow and variable,14 which may lead to altered
115 somatosensory processing and a reorganisation of the sensorimotor cortex with greater reliance being
116 placed on the visual system.57 Diminished proprioceptive ability following ACLR may mean greater
117 error for the athlete when determining how their body is positioned in the environment. Knee
118 proprioception is reduced after ACLR, compared to both the uninjured limb and healthy control limbs,
119 even after rehabilitation and return to sport.42,79,80 Changes in surgical technique to preserve the
120 remnants of the ACL during reconstructive surgery may improve proprioception,7 but the surgical
121 technique is uncommon.
122 Pain and swelling following an ACL injury may inhibit quadriceps activation.81 Knee joint effusion
123 causes activation of afferent pressure receptors within the joint capsule60 due to high intra-articular
124 pressures, and chemical activation of the receptors due to inflammatory cytokines.81 Afferent pressure
125 receptor activations may reduce quadriceps activity64 and strength. 53 Similarly, pain and inflammation
126 can sensitise afferent receptors within the joint capsule and connective tissues, leading to further
127 quadriceps inhibition,60,81 with strength losses of 80-90% within the first few days following knee
128 surgery, which may persist in the weeks after.87 It is therefore essential to measure and monitor
129 athlete pain and effusion throughout the rehabilitation process.
130 Assessment
131 Assessing somatosensory function involves assessing somatosensory cortical processing demands,
132 assessing proprioception, and assessing pain and effusion (Table 1). However, the former generally
133 uses equipment (e.g. functional brain MRI) not readily accessible. Therefore, clinicians should focus
134 on assessing proprioception, pain and effusion.
135 Proprioception
136 Examining proprioceptive function is difficult because it covers several domains: (1) joint position
137 sense, (2) sense of movement (kinaesthesia), (3) sense of movement velocity, and (4) sense of force.75
138 Methods to examine kinaesthesia, sense of velocity and sense of force use specialised tools, such as
139 isokinetic dynamometers. However, joint position sense (JPS) testing is more easily accessible and
140 demonstrates significant proprioceptive impairment in the ACLR limb21,80 and we recommend its use.

142 JPS testing can be split into three broad categories: image/photograph recorded angulation testing,
143 electrogoniometry, and isokinetic dynamometry. While all three approaches can be reliable,19,59,74,78
144 some protocols have poor reliability.90 Larger absolute errors between target angle and athlete’s
145 angle replication attempt indicate JPS deficit. An image-recorded angulation JPS testing method can
146 be easily implemented in the clinic and with good reliability (ICC=0.96-0.98) (Appendix A).77-79 Among
147 10 elites athletes with ACLR, there was a difference of 5.3° in absolute error between the ACLR limb
148 (absolute error= 7.2°) and the uninjured limb (absolute error= 1.9°), reflecting ACLR proprioceptive
149 dysfunction.79. We recommend JPS testing every four to six weeks during rehabilitation.
150 Assessing pain and effusion
151 Regularly assessing joint pain and effusion is essential to minimise potential muscle inhibition,
152 particularly in the quadriceps and hamstrings,54 and to ensure that the athlete’s knee is tolerating
153 rehabilitation program progressions. Numeric rating scale and visual analogue scale are valid and
154 reliable measures, so select a method based on what the athlete prefers.99 A minimal clinically
155 important change in numeric rating scale has not been examined in the ACLR population; it is 2 points
156 in people with chronic musculoskeletal pain.85 The visual analogue scale requires athletes to mark
157 their pain on a 10-centimetre line between ‘0’ (no pain) and ’10 centimetres’ (worst pain imaginable).
158 A minimal clinically important change of 1.4 centimetres is suggested for musculoskeletal conditions
159 and chronic pain.13,39 If pain persists, then consider strategies to manage pain, especially during early
160 stage rehabilitation as pain may inhibit muscle recruitment34 and result in limb off-loading strategies.
161 During mid-to-late stage rehabilitation, pain that negatively affects execution of sporting motor tasks
162 or rehabilitation exercises also needs addressing. Pain assessments should be completed every session
163 with the clinician until the pain resolves to assess how the athlete is responding to their interventions.
164 Measuring effusion following ACL injury is not a direct measure of afferent function but allows
165 clinicians to assess a secondary factor (pressure or inflammation) that may be inhibiting
166 mechanoreceptors within and surrounding the knee. The sweep test and the ballottement test
167 (Appendix B) both have good inter-observer agreement8. Effusion testing should be completed every
168 session the athlete has with the clinician until resolved to ensure that the knee is responding
169 appropriately.
170 Visual system
171 The visual system may be the predominant sensory system used when planning and executing motor
172 tasks.16,23,93 When there is conflict between somatosensory system and visual system afferent
173 information, the visual information takes precedence.70,93 The common thread through theories of
174 how visual information is processed is that the information from the visual system provides the central
175 cortex with information regarding what is in the environment and where it is positioned.16
176 There is limited research examining the changes that occur to the visual system and how visual
177 information is processed following ACL injury. The term visual-motor system encompasses all visual
178 processes and how they influence motor actions.4,23,24,26 Functional brain MRI studies show increased
179 activity in the visual processing cortices following ACLR.27,61 Increased visual processing activity may
180 stem from loss of proprioception during ACL injury and the subsequent effusion and nociception.24
181 Altered afferent information to the sensorimotor cortex leads to reduced postural control, and
182 increased demands on motor planning centres in the frontal lobe and secondary somatosensory
183 cortices (as evidenced by functional brain MRI).6,27,57 To manage reduced postural control and knee
184 afferent input, a re-weighting of the sensory systems may occur with an increased reliance placed on
185 visual information during motor planning and execution.27 This re-weighting potentially contributes to
186 increased cognitive demand which may be detrimental to an athlete by reducing their ability to react
187 quickly to their changing environment.6,37 Given the potential link between increased reliance on the
188 visual-motor system and ACLR reinjury,28 it is important that clinicians assess for potential increased
189 visual reliance.25
190 Assessment
191 Assessment of visual function commonly covers two domains: visual-motor processing ability and
192 increased reliance on the visual-motor system via balance tests (Table 2).
193 Visual-motor processing ability
194 This encompasses all processes that occur from an athlete using their eyes to capture environmental
195 information, the processing of the information in the central cortex and its influence on motor
196 execution.96,97 Poor visual-motor processing ability (visual memory, reaction time and processing
197 speed) may contribute to non-contact ACL injuries as assessed with the ImPACT computer-based
198 neurocognitive test (ImPACT Applications Inc.).95
199 Different companies (e.g. ImPACT [https://impacttest.com/], and Cogstate
200 [https://www.cogstate.com/]) provide computer-based neurocognitive tests that are easy for
201 clinicians to administer at a relatively low cost, even on a large scale. These tests are reliable in
202 uninjured athletes58 but no study has examined their reliability in the ACLR population. A common
203 issue with the neurocognitive tests is that they predominantly test memory and speed of processing
204 domains, with a lack of varied visual-motor domains.
205 ‘Sensory stations’ and tablet systems (e.g. Senaptec, Oregon USA) with visual-motor specific testing
206 make it easier to assess across a number of visual-motor domains that reflect visual acuity (discern
207 shapes and object details), visual memory (store visual information so that learning can occur from
208 previous experiences), near-far eye movements (switch gaze from near to far objects) and multiple
209 object tracking ability (pick up multiple environmental cues)
210 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4Vj78RX7oVo).
211 The sensory station has good reliability in uninjured athletes,17 but no studies have examined its
212 reliability in the ACLR population . While measures of visual-motor performance can predict in-game
213 performances in sports such as professional baseball,41,49 there is currently no research examining
214 ACL injury risk or changes in visual-motor function following injury . As such, there is limited
215 information on what a good baseline score is for each of the visual-motor domains. For the tests to
216 be beneficial, athlete baseline information is required to determine if function has been negatively
217 affected by injury. We have found athletes enjoy engaging in the sensory station due to the novelty
218 and the varied challenging tasks. Their results can be exported as raw scores so that deeper analysis
219 can be conducted. The athlete is provided with an immediate percentile score (against other
220 athletes from similar sports) which drives competition and engagement.

222 Assessing visual-motor reliance via balance tests
223 Balance tests are common in clinical settings to assess an athlete’s ability to integrate sensory
224 (somatosensory, visual and vestibular) information. The athlete performs a task that compares their
225 balance under two conditions: eyes open versus eyes closed. A greater deficit in performance, as
226 compared to either normative data or the uninjured limb, indicates an increased visual-motor system
227 reliance.
228 Postural control worsens when vision is obstructed during single-limb standing in ACL deficient
229 individuals as compared to healthy participants.103 However, the ACLR population exhibits similar
230 reductions in postural control performance as healthy participants (ACLR 43% reduction vs controls
231 45% reduction),103 suggesting that either: (1) visual-motor reliance does not negatively affect an ACLR
232 athlete’s ability to maintain postural control in comparison to healthy controls, or (2) the task of quasi-
233 static standing on one leg may not be challenging enough.
234 We adapted a 20cm stepdown task (Colby et al)9 in which athletes step onto a force plate where they
235 must attain stability as quickly as possible (Appendix C). Athletes complete this with eyes open and
236 then eyes closed, with time to stability used as the outcome measure.5,9 We found good reliability
237 (ICCs= 0.71-0.96) (unpublished) and a visual-motor reliance index score can be ascribed to athletes.
238 Our findings show that healthy athletes improved their time to stability time by 17% with eyes closed.
239 Therefore, if an athlete’s time to stability worsens with eyes closed, we attribute this to visual reliance
240 and suggest they would benefit from targeted rehabilitation strategies. If clinicians do not have access
241 to force plates, subjective assessment of postural control (assessing frontal plane control, trunk sway,
242 hip movement, knee adduction, and foot pronation and supination) may be used to assess athlete
243 performance. We reassess visual-motor reliance every six weeks.
244 Efferent system
245 The main efferent system components involved in motor planning and execution are the motor cortex,
246 descending motor pathway and spinal-reflexive pathways.73,104 After ACL injury, there are changes in
247 all three components,71 which are still evident 6 months following ACLR,44 manifesting in changes in
248 muscle activation, coordination56 and reduced muscle strength.43 This likely contributes (along with
249 muscle atrophy) to persistent quadriceps weakness65,73 and ongoing dysfunction.50,72 Following ACLR,
250 unilateral and bilateral deficits in quadriceps voluntary activation are present up to four years post-
251 surgery.48,71 Deficits in quadriceps activation can result in reduced strength and performance,51 and
252 increased risk of reinjury.69 Although there is some debate,71 the driver of the strength deficit is likely:
253 (1) alterations to the efferent system (motor cortex, descending motor pathway and spinal-reflexive
254 pathways), (2) local muscle atrophy, and (3) negative influences from changes in the sensory system
255 (as previously discussed).
256 Motor cortex
257 The motor cortex (e.g. premotor cortex and primary motor cortex) is involved in movement planning
258 and initiation.47 Following ACLR, there is increased intracortical inhibition associated with reduced
259 voluntary quadriceps activation in the injured limb,52 which can occur bilaterally.105 Subsequently, the
260 athlete needs to dedicate greater neural resources and effort to activate a muscle and execute
261 movement, compared to preinjury, thereby potentially resulting in non-optimal movement
262 strategies.6,25
263 Descending motor pathway
264 The descending motor pathway (corticospinal tract) carries impulses from the motor cortex through
265 the spinal cord to synapse with the lower motor neurone that activates the target muscle.38,84 Its
266 excitability is reduced following ACLR via an increased firing threshold44,71 which may occur in response
267 to increased motor cortex inhibition.29,44 The increased threshold results in reduced quadriceps
268 activation,71 which may change movement strategies.
269 Spinal Reflexive pathways and peripheral changes
270 Spinal reflexive pathways facilitate fast motor responses to peripheral stimuli. ACL injury and ACLR
271 lead to pain, knee joint effusion and loss of proprioceptors within the native ACL,66 which inhibits the
272 quadriceps and increases hamstrings motor activity..36,88 Over time, the excitability of the spinal
273 reflexive pathway to the quadriceps increases such that it is significantly greater in both the ACLR limb
274 and unreconstructed limb in comparison to healthy athletes.83,98
275 All components of the efferent system (motor cortex, descending motor pathway and spinal reflexive
276 pathways) are influenced by ACL injury. An initial reduction in excitability occurs within the spinal
277 reflexive pathways and motor cortex. Reductions in descending motor pathway volume and
278 excitability can then develop, with changes occurring 3-6 months post ACLR.45 These factors may
279 culminate in reduced voluntary activation and function of the quadriceps,71 negatively impacting
280 strength and knee control improvements during rehabilitation.
281 Assessment
282 Assessing the efferent subsystems is primarily conducted with specialised testing equipment and
283 expertise generally unavailable to clinicians. These include Hoffman reflex to assess spinal reflexive
284 changes, transcranial magnetic stimulation to determine corticospinal excitability, and central
285 activation ratio to measure voluntary activation levels of muscles.44 Therefore, clinicians should
286 measure muscle strength and activation (especially the quadriceps) to determine efferent function
287 following ACLR. These tests cannot differentiate which efferent system component is dysfunctional,
288 so management strategies should be generalised to improving overall efferent function (Table 3).

290 Quadriceps and hamstrings strength can be tested via repetition maximum testing (1, 3 or 5 repetition
291 maximum), handheld dynamometry or isokinetic dynamometry. Although they do not provide
292 equivalent measures,18 repetition maximum testing is best placed to examine strength changes
293 through a specific movement such as squats, knee extensions or deadlifts18 which may help clinicians
294 understand if the athlete’s functional patterns are improving. A limitation of using repetition
295 maximum strength testing is that multi-joint movements may improve due to improved inter-
296 segmental coordination, which may mask any lack of improvement in isolated quadriceps strength.
297 Isokinetic dynamometry is the gold standard for examining muscle strength (Appendix D).15,18 It has
298 high reliability (ICC= 0.74 – 0.93)30,91 when assessing quadriceps and hamstrings peak torque. Elite
299 male field-based athletes should be achieving a quadriceps and hamstrings peak torque of 3.19±0.1
300 Nm/kg and 1.78±0.1 Nm/kg; elite female field-based athletes should achieve values of 2.32±0.36
301 Nm/kg and 1.36±0.21Nm/kg.101 In our practice, athletes falling below these levels are prescribed
302 strategies to improve strength and efferent function. Although access to isokinetic dynamometry is
303 improving, it may still be out of reach for many clinicians. Handheld dynamometry is a cost-effective
304 alternative. It is reliable and valid in measuring isometric quadriceps strength when using non-elastic
305 straps.1,46 One disadvantage is that it cannot identify range-specific strength deficits.32 Strength
306 assessments should be completed every 6-8 weeks.
307 Deficits in quadriceps voluntary activation persist following ACLR.48 Surface EMG biofeedback devices
308 are accessible and can determine the magnitude of motor unit recruitment during a contraction,
309 which can give insight into any potential altered efferent function. Commercially available surface
310 EMG biofeedback units (e.g. ‘mTrigger’, LLC, Delaware, USA, and Neurotrac Myo Plus 2, Verity Medical
311 Ltd) have reported that they can compare EMG activity between limbs via dual-channel EMG. The
312 athlete performs 3-6 repetitions of maximal isometric quadriceps activation on the injured and
313 healthy limbs, with the surface electrodes placed over the motor points of the quadriceps. Differences
314 of more than 22%-30% may be clinically-relevant10,67 and can guide clinicians to implement
315 appropriate strategies to improve efferent function.3,92 We suggest assessing every 2 weeks until no
316 significant difference is noted (Appendix E).
317 Summary
318 Sensorimotor dysfunction may persist following ACL injury and occurs across all aspects of the
319 sensorimotor system: afferent pathways, efferent pathways and central processing (Figure 2). We
320 recommend clinicians focus on assessing the somatosensory, visual and efferent systems. Routine
321 assessment of the somatosensory system (JPS testing, pain and effusion testing) and visual system
322 (visual-motor reliance testing and visual-motor processing testing) will guide clinical decisions.
323 Assessing efferent function via strength testing and EMG assessment for voluntary activation can be
324 easily implemented into clinical practice.
Figure 2. Stages of sensorimotor dysfunction occurring following ACL injury and ACLR
325 Key Points
326 Findings: Sensorimotor dysfunction can occur following an ACL injury. It occurs across the
327 somatosensory, visual and efferent systems.
328 Implications: All three systems should be assessed: somatosensory (JPS, pain and effusion tests),
329 visual system (visual-motor reliance and visual-motor processing tests), and efferent system
330 (strength and voluntary activation tests)
331 Caution: More research is required for visual-motor reliance and visual-motor processing tests to
332 identify normative values, and to determine if they are related to reinjury

42	31 Abstract
43	32 Background. Sensorimotor dysfunction following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and
44	33 subsequent ACL reconstruction (ACLR) may lead to errors in motor planning and execution.
45	34 Dysfunction occurs even after athletes have completed rehabilitation. Therefore, clinicians need to
46	35 implement strategies to improve how sensorimotor dysfunction is addressed during rehabilitation.
47	36 Clinical question. How can clinicians improve their rehabilitation of sensorimotor dysfunction
48	37 following ACLR? The aim of this clinical commentary is to review methods that may improve
49	38 rehabilitation by targeting sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury.
50	39 Key results. Rehabilitation should focus on two priorities: (1) improving peripheral and central
51	40 efferent function, and (2) improving somatosensory function and reducing reliance on the visual-
52	41 motor system.
53	42 Clinical application. Somatosensory function can improve with proprioceptive training but should be
54	43 implemented within the first six weeks of injury/surgery to minimise the chance of increased
55	44 reliance on the visual-motor system. Methods to increase the complexity of proprioceptive training
56	45 includes varying the: (1) type of task (e.g. jumping, decelerating, etc), (2) the visual information used
57	46 during the task, (3) the cognitive loading during the task, and (4) perturbations. Visual distraction
58	47 training may be useful for challenging an athlete during sports-specific training and reduce the
59	48 reliance on the visual-motor system. Improving peripheral and central efferent function involves
60	49 using regular cryotherapy and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) in the early stages
61	50 to minimise pain and improve muscle recruitment. Throughout rehabilitation, strength training,
62	51 neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) and surface EMG biofeedback methods improve
63	52 central and peripheral efferent function when prescribed at a high intensity.
64	53 Key words
65	54 Anterior cruciate ligament, sensorimotor dysfunction, treatment, rehabilitation, afferent, efferent
66	3
67	55 Introduction
68	56 Sensorimotor dysfunction can persist after rehabilitation, leading to errors in motor planning and
69	57 execution,25,56 as described in Part 1.61 Rehabilitation following ACLR focuses on: (1) achieving a
70	58 ‘calm’ knee joint (full ROM and no effusion) early post-surgery, (2) regaining strength and power, (3)
71	59 introducing linear and multi-directional running, and (4) reintroducing sport.60 With lingering
72	60 sensorimotor dysfunction, it is possible that clinicians may not be using effective strategies to target
73	61 these specific deficits. The aim of this clinical commentary is to review methods that may improve
74	62 rehabilitation by targeting sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury and ACLR. We include
75	63 evidence-based suggestions that are driven by our clinical practice in a sports medicine facility and
76	64 mechanistic research. Key definitions are listed in Table 1.
77	Table 1. Key terms related to sensorimotor dysfunction
78	Term Definition
79	Sensorimotor A system integral to motor control within the body that encompasses
80	afferent, efferent and central processing pathways
81	Efferent Includes pathways that takes neural activity to the muscles to create
82	movement
83	Central efferent function Focuses on efferent activity within the brain
84	Peripheral efferent Focuses on efferent activity in the descending motor column and spinal
85	function reflexive activity
86	Afferent Includes pathways that takes neural activity from the sensory systems to
87	the brain
88	Somatosensory Sensory system focused on perception of position, movement, touch
89	pressure and pain
90	Proprioception A function of the somatosensory system that relates to the body’s
91	ability to sense position of its body segments in space
92	65 Clinical question
93	66 How can clinicians improve their rehabilitation of sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury?
94	67 Dysfunction within the afferent and efferent pathways following ACL injury and ACLR are
95	68 summarised in Figure 1.61 The two events that are pertinent to clinicians are: (1) reduced efferent
96	69 function, and (2) increased reliance on the visual-motor system (figure 1). The reduced efferent
97	70 function results from reduced central and peripheral efferent factors. Increased reliance on the
98	4
99	71 visual-motor system occurs in response to altered somatosensory function, namely altered
100	72 proprioceptive information following the damage to proprioceptors within the ACL. Therefore,
101	73 clinicians should focus their rehabilitation on the following areas to effectively manage sensorimotor
102	74 dysfunction (figure 1):
103	75 1. Improving peripheral and central efferent function
104	76 2. Improving somatosensory function and reducing reliance on the visual-motor system
105	77 The following sections review the methods of rehabilitation targeting the above priorities and
106	78 providing guidelines for how clinicians may implement these in practice.
107	5
108	Reduced somatosensory
109	function
110	Increased visual-motor Reduced peripheral and
111	FIGURE 1. Sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury and ACLR. Also outlines thecentral
112	reliance efferentfor
113	two priorities function
114	clinicians rehabilitating athletes with sensorimotor dysfunction.
115	6
116	79 Improving peripheral and central efferent function
117	80 Improving peripheral and central efferent function is important to ensure complete restoration of
118	81 strength and to avoid developing any compensatory changes to an athlete’s movement technique.
119	82 Peripheral efferent dysfunction is predominantly found in the first few weeks post-injury which
120	83 reduces spinal reflex excitability. Central efferent dysfunction manifests as descending motor
121	84 inhibition sub-acutely following surgery.34,50
122	85 Early-stage rehabilitation after ACLR
123	86 Knee joint pain and swelling reduces the spinal-reflexive pathway and quadriceps activation.30,48
124	87 Regular movement of the knee, lower limb strength exercises and gait retraining must be completed
125	88 early in rehabilitation to help to reduce pain and swelling in the knee.31 However, additional
126	89 strategies to improve pain and swelling should be used aggressively in the early stages of
127	90 rehabilitation to augment recovery. Methods include pain medication, transcutaneous electrical
128	91 nerve stimulation (TENS) and cryotherapy.55
129	92 Pain medication strategies can vary. Post-operative pain is generally at its worst in the first three
130	93 days and nerve blocks are often used to reduce the pain and allow early ambulation and discharge.7
131	94 Nerve blocks reduce post-operative pain and analgesic use.16 Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory
132	95 medications are common in outpatient care.8 They reduce pain and the need for analgesic
133	96 medication following ACLR.53 Any medication should be appropriately prescribed by the treating
134	97 physician and surgeon within the scope of their respective regulatory bodies.
135	98 TENS devices apply an electrical impulse to the large diameter afferent nerve fibres via electrodes
136	99 placed around the injured structure.51 The afferent information is processed in the central cortex
137	100 which activates descending inhibitory pathways, resulting in a reduction in peripheral and central
138	101 hyperalgesia.19 TENS can reduce knee pain by 36% if the dosage is set to: a strong non-noxious
139	102 stimulus, low frequency setting of 1-8Hz, high frequency of 25-120Hz, 20 minutes treatment time
140	103 and at least 5 treatment sessions.6
141	7
142	104 Cryotherapy reduces pain and the need for analgesic medication.40,52 Cryotherapy devices, especially
143	105 those with pneumatic pressure to provide compression to the knee, such as ‘Game Ready’
144	106 (CoolSystems Inc, USA) and ‘Cryocuff IC Cooler’ (DonJoy Global, USA), reduce pain significantly more
145	107 than ice packs alone.46,62 Cryotherapy-compression significantly reduced participants’ pain (by 50%)
146	108 and led to the cessation of pain medication (83% of participants ceased medication by 6 weeks) as
147	109 compared to no significant change in pain in those using standard ice packs and only a small portion
148	110 of these participants ceasing pain medication (23% of participants ceased medication by 6 weeks).62
149	111 In summary, to improve efferent function in the early stages of rehabilitation, clinicians may choose
150	112 to recommend regular cryotherapy with compression devices (ideally three times a day or once a
151	113 day if there are accessibility barriers) for the first 6 weeks post-operative and apply TENS daily for 20
152	114 minutes for the first 4-6 weeks.
153	115 Throughout rehabilitation
154	116 Strength training is a mainstay of ACLR rehabilitation and provides a powerful stimulus to improve
155	117 peripheral and central efferent function. In the uninjured population, strength training increases
156	118 motor unit excitation and recruitment, increases corticospinal excitability and reduces intracortical
157	119 inhibition.21,28,41 Changes in neural excitability occur within strength training sessions and can be
158	120 maintained between sessions.41 Why is efferent dysfunction is measured so commonly in ACLR
159	121 individuals who have participated in strength training?34,36,50 Training intensity is a key factor in
160	122 improving corticospinal excitability.10 There are significant increases in corticospinal excitability
161	123 when participants train at 75% of maximum voluntary contraction, and no changes at 25% of
162	124 maximum voluntary contraction. A progressive resistance program (resistance built up overtime to
163	125 >90% of 1 repetition maximum) increased the quadriceps and hamstrings strength of ACLR athletes
164	126 to the same level as healthy controls by 7 months post-surgery.63 Therefore, training intensity is
165	127 important during ACLR rehabilitation and previous research may not have trained participants at
166	8
167	128 sufficiently high intensity to achieve symmetrical strength and to improve their efferent function
168	129 back to baseline.
169	130 Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) and surface electromyography (EMG) biofeedback can
170	131 be used as adjuncts to strength training to improve efferent function.11,23 NMES commonly uses a
171	132 handheld device to apply an electrical current to muscles via electrodes placed on the skin (e.g.
172	133 ‘Compex’, DonJoy Global, USA and ‘Neurotrac Sport’, Verity Medical Ltd, UK). The electrical current
173	134 elicits a contraction in the muscle. Because athletes in early rehabilitation have diminished spinal
174	135 reflexive activity and reduced voluntary quadriceps activation,34 NMES provides an avenue to
175	136 contract the quadriceps without the risk of heavy loads going through the joint if the athlete was to
176	137 otherwise perform a high intensity strength exercise. NMES also preferentially recruits type II muscle
177	138 fibres which may minimise the risk of selective atrophy of the these muscle fibres 37,59 and improve
178	139 quadriceps force production.26 NMES in addition to exercises and physiotherapy results in
179	140 significantly better quadriceps strength when compared to exercises and physiotherapy alone.13,26,64
180	141 NMES was mainly effective when used at high intensities with the contraction time set to 15-20
181	142 seconds and rest time set to 15-50 seconds.17,54 NMES was generally used 5-7 days per week for the
182	143 first 4-12 weeks post-ACLR but the frequency of this may need to be reduced if accessibility barriers
183	144 exist for athletes.17,22,54
184	145 Surface EMG biofeedback devices are commonly handheld devices, with electrodes placed over the
185	146 motor units of the target muscles (e.g. ‘Neurotrac Simplex’, Verity Medical Ltd, UK and ‘mTrigger’,
186	147 LLC, Delaware, USA). They measure the magnitude of motor unit recruitment and provide that
187	148 information to the user on an easy-to-read display. The clinician can set a target for muscle activity
188	149 for the athlete to achieve, and the athlete receives an auditory or visual stimulus each time that they
189	150 achieve the goal. This differs from NMES which is best used as a passive modality. EMG biofeedback
190	151 training provides an external focus of attention to their training and can improve corticospinal
191	152 excitability, which is otherwise unaffected by NMES.49 EMG biofeedback training increases
192	9
193	153 quadriceps strength,12,35 and can be completed with isometric and isotonic exercises.2,65 A dosage of
194	154 5-7 days per week2,29 is effective in improving strength. However, accessibility barriers for athletes
195	155 may mean this frequency is not possible. Athletes may find it easier to focus on using EMG
196	156 biofeedback training during their strength sessions.
197	157 In summary (Figure 2), improving efferent function via improving spinal reflexive activity,
198	158 corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability is essential throughout rehabilitation.
199	159 Progressive strength training at a sufficient intensity (>75% of 1 repetition max) to elicit strength and
200	160 hypertrophy changes, is a powerful stimulus to all components of the efferent system. NMES could
201	161 be used during the first 6 weeks post-surgery to minimise type II muscle fibre atrophy in the
202	162 quadriceps37,59 and to maintain or increase spinal reflexive activity to the quadriceps that would
203	163 otherwise be inhibited due to the pain and swelling. As the swelling reduces and the athlete can
204	164 voluntarily activate their quadriceps, reduce NMES to non-strength training days (once or twice a
205	165 day depending on accessibility barriers of the athlete) and as part of the warmup on a strength
206	166 session (5-10 minutes in preparation part of session). The athlete may also add EMG biofeedback
207	167 training to their program during strength sessions until there are no clinically relevant strength or
208	168 efferent deficit between limbs.
209	10
210	FIGURE 2. Take home messages for clinicians regarding treatment modalities.
211	Abbreviations: TENS= transcutaneous electrical stimulation, NMES= neuromuscular electrical
212	stimulation, mins= minutes, Hz= Hertz, s= seconds, RM= repetition maximum
213	169 Improving somatosensory function and reducing reliance on the visual-motor system
214	170 Improving somatosensory function early in rehabilitation is essential to restoring normal function,
215	171 reducing re-injury risk, and minimising reliance on the visual-motor system.24 Somatosensory
216	172 dysfunction primarily results from the loss of afferent feedback from the ACL and secondarily from
217	173 pain and swelling. Therefore, early rehabilitation strategies should focus on improving an athlete’s
218	174 proprioceptive ability and reducing pain and swelling. Regrowth of the proprioceptor nerve fibres
219	175 into the ACL graft can take months, with no exact time period identified.4,18 Therefore, improving an
220	176 athlete’s proprioceptive ability in early-stage rehabilitation primarily focuses on improving the
221	177 control of the surrounding muscles and joints to compensate lack of proprioceptive information
222	178 from the ACL graft. In the case of non-operatively managed ACL injuries, this focus on control of the
223	11
224	179 surrounding muscles and joints needs to be completed throughout rehabilitation as the remaining
225	180 proprioceptors in the ACL stump may provide altered information.18,20
226	181 Proprioceptive training focuses on using somatosensory afferent information in the absence of
227	182 vision.1 Proprioceptive training significantly improved proprioceptive ability across a range of
228	183 injuries, including knee pathology.1 While proprioceptive training reduces the incidence of ACL
229	184 primary injury in field-based athletes,14,32,38 there is a lack of research following ACLR to determine
230	185 its effectiveness.
231	186 Implementing proprioceptive training very early in rehabilitation is likely important as reliance on
232	187 the visual-motor system occurs within the first six weeks after surgery.33 Proprioceptive training in
233	188 the clinic predominantly takes the form of balance exercises. Program proprioceptive training such
234	189 that the complexity of the drill progressively increases. Complexity can be progressed by (Figure 3):
235	190 (1) the type of task (e.g. stationary standing or a landing task), (2) the amount of visual information
236	191 (e.g. full vision, blinded vision or partial blinding), (3) the amount of cognitive loading (e.g. dual task
237	192 loading and cognitive task) and (4) the amount of perturbation (e.g. foam surface or external
238	193 perturbation application).
239	12
240	FIGURE 3. Framework outlining factors that need to be considered when creating
241	194
242	proprioceptive drills: type of task, visual information, cognitive loading and perturbation.
243	195
244	196 Factor 1- Type of task
245	197 Many of the tasks used for proprioceptive training are low-load and low-velocity in nature, such as
246	198 single-leg standing or squatting. As rehabilitation progresses, exercises need to progress into higher
247	199 loads and velocities in multiple movement planes, such as stepping tasks, landing tasks, deceleration
248	200 tasks and change of direction tasks (Figure 3).
249	13
250	201 Factor 2- Visual information
251	202 Maintaining postural control or executing a movement requires the athlete to process
252	203 somatosensory and visual information so that appropriate muscle actions can be executed.27 If visual
253	204 information is removed, then the athlete will rely more on proprioception. Clinicians commonly
254	205 remove vision during a proprioception drill (e.g. standing on one leg eye closed). As the task
255	206 progresses to a more dynamic task, such as a landing task, being blinded may make the task too
256	207 difficult to complete or dangerous. A method that can be used to reduce visual information is the
257	208 use of stroboscopic glasses (e.g. ‘Senaptec’, Oregon USA). Training with stroboscopic glasses
258	209 facilitates motor skill acquisition.5
259	210 Stroboscopic glasses flicker between being transparent and opaque so that visual information is
260	211 partially reduced. The frequency with which the glasses flicker can be altered by clinicians so a single
261	212 task can have several levels of difficulty. An example is an athlete being tasked to jump and land on a
262	213 single leg. Initially the task can be completed with a high frequency on the stroboscopic glasses
263	214 (more visual information available) and as the athlete progresses, the frequency is reduced so that
264	215 there are longer periods of opacity (less visual information available).
265	216 The ideal dosage for stroboscopic training in the ACLR population is unclear. Training dosage in
266	217 studies investigating skill acquisition vary from short (ten minutes) daily sessions to longer (30-50
267	218 minutes) sessions two to three times per week.3,15,44 We have found three sessions per week with
268	219 stroboscopic glasses is most practical in exposing athletes to this training. Glasses with pinholes or
269	220 shutters can substitute for stroboscopic glasses, although may not be as effective.
270	221 Factor 3- Cognitive loading
271	222 ACL injuries occur in chaotic sporting environments. Athletes need to coordinate movements while
272	223 processing multiple stimuli (e.g. position of opponents and position on the field) and making
273	224 multiple decisions (e.g. state of the game, whether to pass and remembering gameplay instructions).
274	14
275	225 These factors add to the cognitive burden in athletes and may lead to errors in movement
276	226 coordination and execution.56 It is important that clinicians progressively add cognitive load to
277	227 proprioceptive tasks during rehabilitation.9,57,58 Cognitive load can be made in the form of: (1)
278	228 reaction to a stimulus, (2) memory task, (3) decision making task, (4) calculations or (5) a
279	229 combination of the 4 forms (Figure 3).
280	230 Factor 4- Perturbation
281	231 Perturbations are unexpected forces applied to the athlete to induce a reactive control of posture.42
282	232 Drills incorporating perturbation should meet two conditions: (1) the external perturbation should
283	233 induce a rapid and sudden motor response and (2) the perturbation should cause a loss of stability
284	234 (e.g. a stumble or fall) without a sufficient motor response.42 Perturbation training is effective in
285	235 improving balance following ACL injury,43 chronic ankle instability45,47 and preventing falls.39
286	236 Examples of drills using varying degrees of perturbation are in Figure 3. Examples of how to progress
287	237 single leg balance, single leg hop and change of direction drills are shown in supplementary videos 1-
288	238 3.
289	239 Summary
290	240 The two goals of rehabilitation are: (1) to improve peripheral and central efferent function, and (2)
291	241 to improve somatosensory function and reduce the reliance on the visual-motor system. There is
292	242 strong evidence for using strength training, NMES and surface EMG biofeedback to improve efferent
293	243 function. While these methods are effective in improving efferent function, clinicians must take care
294	244 to prescribe the interventions at the appropriate intensity to achieve best results. There is good
295	245 evidence for proprioceptive training, TENS and cryotherapy to improve somatosensory function.
296	246 However, there is a lack of evidence examining whether these interventions reduce reliance on the
297	247 visual-motor system. Increasing the complexity of proprioceptive training across type of task,
298	15
299	248 amount of visual information, cognitive loading and perturbations may help to improve the
300	249 effectiveness of proprioceptive training in reducing visual-motor reliance.
301	250 Key Points
302	251 Findings: To improve sensorimotor function following ACL injury, clinicians could aim to (1) improve
303	252 peripheral and central efferent function and (2) improve somatosensory function and reduce
304	253 reliance on the visual-motor system. Interventions can be implemented early in rehabilitation and
305	254 progressed over time.
306	255 Implications: Clinicians can use strength training, NMES and surface EMG biofeedback to improve
307	256 local and central efferent function. Improving somatosensory function can be achieved through
308	257 proprioceptive training, TENS and cryotherapy.
309	258 Caution: There is a lack of prospective research to identify if proprioceptive training can reduce
310	259 visual-motor reliance.

31 Abstract
32 Background. Sensorimotor dysfunction following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and
33 subsequent ACL reconstruction (ACLR) may lead to errors in motor planning and execution.
34 Dysfunction occurs even after athletes have completed rehabilitation. Therefore, clinicians need to
35 implement strategies to improve how sensorimotor dysfunction is addressed during rehabilitation.
36 Clinical question. How can clinicians improve their rehabilitation of sensorimotor dysfunction
37 following ACLR? The aim of this clinical commentary is to review methods that may improve
38 rehabilitation by targeting sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury.
39 Key results. Rehabilitation should focus on two priorities: (1) improving peripheral and central
40 efferent function, and (2) improving somatosensory function and reducing reliance on the visual-
41 motor system.
42 Clinical application. Somatosensory function can improve with proprioceptive training but should be
43 implemented within the first six weeks of injury/surgery to minimise the chance of increased
44 reliance on the visual-motor system. Methods to increase the complexity of proprioceptive training
45 includes varying the: (1) type of task (e.g. jumping, decelerating, etc), (2) the visual information used
46 during the task, (3) the cognitive loading during the task, and (4) perturbations. Visual distraction
47 training may be useful for challenging an athlete during sports-specific training and reduce the
48 reliance on the visual-motor system. Improving peripheral and central efferent function involves
49 using regular cryotherapy and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) in the early stages
50 to minimise pain and improve muscle recruitment. Throughout rehabilitation, strength training,
51 neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) and surface EMG biofeedback methods improve
52 central and peripheral efferent function when prescribed at a high intensity.
53 Key words
54 Anterior cruciate ligament, sensorimotor dysfunction, treatment, rehabilitation, afferent, efferent
3
55 Introduction
56 Sensorimotor dysfunction can persist after rehabilitation, leading to errors in motor planning and
57 execution,25,56 as described in Part 1.61 Rehabilitation following ACLR focuses on: (1) achieving a
58 ‘calm’ knee joint (full ROM and no effusion) early post-surgery, (2) regaining strength and power, (3)
59 introducing linear and multi-directional running, and (4) reintroducing sport.60 With lingering
60 sensorimotor dysfunction, it is possible that clinicians may not be using effective strategies to target
61 these specific deficits. The aim of this clinical commentary is to review methods that may improve
62 rehabilitation by targeting sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury and ACLR. We include
63 evidence-based suggestions that are driven by our clinical practice in a sports medicine facility and
64 mechanistic research. Key definitions are listed in Table 1.
Table 1. Key terms related to sensorimotor dysfunction
Term Definition
Sensorimotor A system integral to motor control within the body that encompasses
afferent, efferent and central processing pathways
Efferent Includes pathways that takes neural activity to the muscles to create
movement
Central efferent function Focuses on efferent activity within the brain
Peripheral efferent Focuses on efferent activity in the descending motor column and spinal
function reflexive activity
Afferent Includes pathways that takes neural activity from the sensory systems to
the brain
Somatosensory Sensory system focused on perception of position, movement, touch
pressure and pain
Proprioception A function of the somatosensory system that relates to the body’s
ability to sense position of its body segments in space
65 Clinical question
66 How can clinicians improve their rehabilitation of sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury?
67 Dysfunction within the afferent and efferent pathways following ACL injury and ACLR are
68 summarised in Figure 1.61 The two events that are pertinent to clinicians are: (1) reduced efferent
69 function, and (2) increased reliance on the visual-motor system (figure 1). The reduced efferent
70 function results from reduced central and peripheral efferent factors. Increased reliance on the
4
71 visual-motor system occurs in response to altered somatosensory function, namely altered
72 proprioceptive information following the damage to proprioceptors within the ACL. Therefore,
73 clinicians should focus their rehabilitation on the following areas to effectively manage sensorimotor
74 dysfunction (figure 1):
75 1. Improving peripheral and central efferent function
76 2. Improving somatosensory function and reducing reliance on the visual-motor system
77 The following sections review the methods of rehabilitation targeting the above priorities and
78 providing guidelines for how clinicians may implement these in practice.
5
Reduced somatosensory
function
Increased visual-motor Reduced peripheral and
FIGURE 1. Sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL injury and ACLR. Also outlines thecentral
reliance efferentfor
two priorities function
clinicians rehabilitating athletes with sensorimotor dysfunction.
6
79 Improving peripheral and central efferent function
80 Improving peripheral and central efferent function is important to ensure complete restoration of
81 strength and to avoid developing any compensatory changes to an athlete’s movement technique.
82 Peripheral efferent dysfunction is predominantly found in the first few weeks post-injury which
83 reduces spinal reflex excitability. Central efferent dysfunction manifests as descending motor
84 inhibition sub-acutely following surgery.34,50
85 Early-stage rehabilitation after ACLR
86 Knee joint pain and swelling reduces the spinal-reflexive pathway and quadriceps activation.30,48
87 Regular movement of the knee, lower limb strength exercises and gait retraining must be completed
88 early in rehabilitation to help to reduce pain and swelling in the knee.31 However, additional
89 strategies to improve pain and swelling should be used aggressively in the early stages of
90 rehabilitation to augment recovery. Methods include pain medication, transcutaneous electrical
91 nerve stimulation (TENS) and cryotherapy.55
92 Pain medication strategies can vary. Post-operative pain is generally at its worst in the first three
93 days and nerve blocks are often used to reduce the pain and allow early ambulation and discharge.7
94 Nerve blocks reduce post-operative pain and analgesic use.16 Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory
95 medications are common in outpatient care.8 They reduce pain and the need for analgesic
96 medication following ACLR.53 Any medication should be appropriately prescribed by the treating
97 physician and surgeon within the scope of their respective regulatory bodies.
98 TENS devices apply an electrical impulse to the large diameter afferent nerve fibres via electrodes
99 placed around the injured structure.51 The afferent information is processed in the central cortex
100 which activates descending inhibitory pathways, resulting in a reduction in peripheral and central
101 hyperalgesia.19 TENS can reduce knee pain by 36% if the dosage is set to: a strong non-noxious
102 stimulus, low frequency setting of 1-8Hz, high frequency of 25-120Hz, 20 minutes treatment time
103 and at least 5 treatment sessions.6
7
104 Cryotherapy reduces pain and the need for analgesic medication.40,52 Cryotherapy devices, especially
105 those with pneumatic pressure to provide compression to the knee, such as ‘Game Ready’
106 (CoolSystems Inc, USA) and ‘Cryocuff IC Cooler’ (DonJoy Global, USA), reduce pain significantly more
107 than ice packs alone.46,62 Cryotherapy-compression significantly reduced participants’ pain (by 50%)
108 and led to the cessation of pain medication (83% of participants ceased medication by 6 weeks) as
109 compared to no significant change in pain in those using standard ice packs and only a small portion
110 of these participants ceasing pain medication (23% of participants ceased medication by 6 weeks).62
111 In summary, to improve efferent function in the early stages of rehabilitation, clinicians may choose
112 to recommend regular cryotherapy with compression devices (ideally three times a day or once a
113 day if there are accessibility barriers) for the first 6 weeks post-operative and apply TENS daily for 20
114 minutes for the first 4-6 weeks.
115 Throughout rehabilitation
116 Strength training is a mainstay of ACLR rehabilitation and provides a powerful stimulus to improve
117 peripheral and central efferent function. In the uninjured population, strength training increases
118 motor unit excitation and recruitment, increases corticospinal excitability and reduces intracortical
119 inhibition.21,28,41 Changes in neural excitability occur within strength training sessions and can be
120 maintained between sessions.41 Why is efferent dysfunction is measured so commonly in ACLR
121 individuals who have participated in strength training?34,36,50 Training intensity is a key factor in
122 improving corticospinal excitability.10 There are significant increases in corticospinal excitability
123 when participants train at 75% of maximum voluntary contraction, and no changes at 25% of
124 maximum voluntary contraction. A progressive resistance program (resistance built up overtime to
125 >90% of 1 repetition maximum) increased the quadriceps and hamstrings strength of ACLR athletes
126 to the same level as healthy controls by 7 months post-surgery.63 Therefore, training intensity is
127 important during ACLR rehabilitation and previous research may not have trained participants at
8
128 sufficiently high intensity to achieve symmetrical strength and to improve their efferent function
129 back to baseline.
130 Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) and surface electromyography (EMG) biofeedback can
131 be used as adjuncts to strength training to improve efferent function.11,23 NMES commonly uses a
132 handheld device to apply an electrical current to muscles via electrodes placed on the skin (e.g.
133 ‘Compex’, DonJoy Global, USA and ‘Neurotrac Sport’, Verity Medical Ltd, UK). The electrical current
134 elicits a contraction in the muscle. Because athletes in early rehabilitation have diminished spinal
135 reflexive activity and reduced voluntary quadriceps activation,34 NMES provides an avenue to
136 contract the quadriceps without the risk of heavy loads going through the joint if the athlete was to
137 otherwise perform a high intensity strength exercise. NMES also preferentially recruits type II muscle
138 fibres which may minimise the risk of selective atrophy of the these muscle fibres 37,59 and improve
139 quadriceps force production.26 NMES in addition to exercises and physiotherapy results in
140 significantly better quadriceps strength when compared to exercises and physiotherapy alone.13,26,64
141 NMES was mainly effective when used at high intensities with the contraction time set to 15-20
142 seconds and rest time set to 15-50 seconds.17,54 NMES was generally used 5-7 days per week for the
143 first 4-12 weeks post-ACLR but the frequency of this may need to be reduced if accessibility barriers
144 exist for athletes.17,22,54
145 Surface EMG biofeedback devices are commonly handheld devices, with electrodes placed over the
146 motor units of the target muscles (e.g. ‘Neurotrac Simplex’, Verity Medical Ltd, UK and ‘mTrigger’,
147 LLC, Delaware, USA). They measure the magnitude of motor unit recruitment and provide that
148 information to the user on an easy-to-read display. The clinician can set a target for muscle activity
149 for the athlete to achieve, and the athlete receives an auditory or visual stimulus each time that they
150 achieve the goal. This differs from NMES which is best used as a passive modality. EMG biofeedback
151 training provides an external focus of attention to their training and can improve corticospinal
152 excitability, which is otherwise unaffected by NMES.49 EMG biofeedback training increases
9
153 quadriceps strength,12,35 and can be completed with isometric and isotonic exercises.2,65 A dosage of
154 5-7 days per week2,29 is effective in improving strength. However, accessibility barriers for athletes
155 may mean this frequency is not possible. Athletes may find it easier to focus on using EMG
156 biofeedback training during their strength sessions.
157 In summary (Figure 2), improving efferent function via improving spinal reflexive activity,
158 corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability is essential throughout rehabilitation.
159 Progressive strength training at a sufficient intensity (>75% of 1 repetition max) to elicit strength and
160 hypertrophy changes, is a powerful stimulus to all components of the efferent system. NMES could
161 be used during the first 6 weeks post-surgery to minimise type II muscle fibre atrophy in the
162 quadriceps37,59 and to maintain or increase spinal reflexive activity to the quadriceps that would
163 otherwise be inhibited due to the pain and swelling. As the swelling reduces and the athlete can
164 voluntarily activate their quadriceps, reduce NMES to non-strength training days (once or twice a
165 day depending on accessibility barriers of the athlete) and as part of the warmup on a strength
166 session (5-10 minutes in preparation part of session). The athlete may also add EMG biofeedback
167 training to their program during strength sessions until there are no clinically relevant strength or
168 efferent deficit between limbs.
10
FIGURE 2. Take home messages for clinicians regarding treatment modalities.
Abbreviations: TENS= transcutaneous electrical stimulation, NMES= neuromuscular electrical
stimulation, mins= minutes, Hz= Hertz, s= seconds, RM= repetition maximum
169 Improving somatosensory function and reducing reliance on the visual-motor system
170 Improving somatosensory function early in rehabilitation is essential to restoring normal function,
171 reducing re-injury risk, and minimising reliance on the visual-motor system.24 Somatosensory
172 dysfunction primarily results from the loss of afferent feedback from the ACL and secondarily from
173 pain and swelling. Therefore, early rehabilitation strategies should focus on improving an athlete’s
174 proprioceptive ability and reducing pain and swelling. Regrowth of the proprioceptor nerve fibres
175 into the ACL graft can take months, with no exact time period identified.4,18 Therefore, improving an
176 athlete’s proprioceptive ability in early-stage rehabilitation primarily focuses on improving the
177 control of the surrounding muscles and joints to compensate lack of proprioceptive information
178 from the ACL graft. In the case of non-operatively managed ACL injuries, this focus on control of the
11
179 surrounding muscles and joints needs to be completed throughout rehabilitation as the remaining
180 proprioceptors in the ACL stump may provide altered information.18,20
181 Proprioceptive training focuses on using somatosensory afferent information in the absence of
182 vision.1 Proprioceptive training significantly improved proprioceptive ability across a range of
183 injuries, including knee pathology.1 While proprioceptive training reduces the incidence of ACL
184 primary injury in field-based athletes,14,32,38 there is a lack of research following ACLR to determine
185 its effectiveness.
186 Implementing proprioceptive training very early in rehabilitation is likely important as reliance on
187 the visual-motor system occurs within the first six weeks after surgery.33 Proprioceptive training in
188 the clinic predominantly takes the form of balance exercises. Program proprioceptive training such
189 that the complexity of the drill progressively increases. Complexity can be progressed by (Figure 3):
190 (1) the type of task (e.g. stationary standing or a landing task), (2) the amount of visual information
191 (e.g. full vision, blinded vision or partial blinding), (3) the amount of cognitive loading (e.g. dual task
192 loading and cognitive task) and (4) the amount of perturbation (e.g. foam surface or external
193 perturbation application).
12
FIGURE 3. Framework outlining factors that need to be considered when creating
194
proprioceptive drills: type of task, visual information, cognitive loading and perturbation.
195
196 Factor 1- Type of task
197 Many of the tasks used for proprioceptive training are low-load and low-velocity in nature, such as
198 single-leg standing or squatting. As rehabilitation progresses, exercises need to progress into higher
199 loads and velocities in multiple movement planes, such as stepping tasks, landing tasks, deceleration
200 tasks and change of direction tasks (Figure 3).
13
201 Factor 2- Visual information
202 Maintaining postural control or executing a movement requires the athlete to process
203 somatosensory and visual information so that appropriate muscle actions can be executed.27 If visual
204 information is removed, then the athlete will rely more on proprioception. Clinicians commonly
205 remove vision during a proprioception drill (e.g. standing on one leg eye closed). As the task
206 progresses to a more dynamic task, such as a landing task, being blinded may make the task too
207 difficult to complete or dangerous. A method that can be used to reduce visual information is the
208 use of stroboscopic glasses (e.g. ‘Senaptec’, Oregon USA). Training with stroboscopic glasses
209 facilitates motor skill acquisition.5
210 Stroboscopic glasses flicker between being transparent and opaque so that visual information is
211 partially reduced. The frequency with which the glasses flicker can be altered by clinicians so a single
212 task can have several levels of difficulty. An example is an athlete being tasked to jump and land on a
213 single leg. Initially the task can be completed with a high frequency on the stroboscopic glasses
214 (more visual information available) and as the athlete progresses, the frequency is reduced so that
215 there are longer periods of opacity (less visual information available).
216 The ideal dosage for stroboscopic training in the ACLR population is unclear. Training dosage in
217 studies investigating skill acquisition vary from short (ten minutes) daily sessions to longer (30-50
218 minutes) sessions two to three times per week.3,15,44 We have found three sessions per week with
219 stroboscopic glasses is most practical in exposing athletes to this training. Glasses with pinholes or
220 shutters can substitute for stroboscopic glasses, although may not be as effective.
221 Factor 3- Cognitive loading
222 ACL injuries occur in chaotic sporting environments. Athletes need to coordinate movements while
223 processing multiple stimuli (e.g. position of opponents and position on the field) and making
224 multiple decisions (e.g. state of the game, whether to pass and remembering gameplay instructions).
14
225 These factors add to the cognitive burden in athletes and may lead to errors in movement
226 coordination and execution.56 It is important that clinicians progressively add cognitive load to
227 proprioceptive tasks during rehabilitation.9,57,58 Cognitive load can be made in the form of: (1)
228 reaction to a stimulus, (2) memory task, (3) decision making task, (4) calculations or (5) a
229 combination of the 4 forms (Figure 3).
230 Factor 4- Perturbation
231 Perturbations are unexpected forces applied to the athlete to induce a reactive control of posture.42
232 Drills incorporating perturbation should meet two conditions: (1) the external perturbation should
233 induce a rapid and sudden motor response and (2) the perturbation should cause a loss of stability
234 (e.g. a stumble or fall) without a sufficient motor response.42 Perturbation training is effective in
235 improving balance following ACL injury,43 chronic ankle instability45,47 and preventing falls.39
236 Examples of drills using varying degrees of perturbation are in Figure 3. Examples of how to progress
237 single leg balance, single leg hop and change of direction drills are shown in supplementary videos 1-
238 3.
239 Summary
240 The two goals of rehabilitation are: (1) to improve peripheral and central efferent function, and (2)
241 to improve somatosensory function and reduce the reliance on the visual-motor system. There is
242 strong evidence for using strength training, NMES and surface EMG biofeedback to improve efferent
243 function. While these methods are effective in improving efferent function, clinicians must take care
244 to prescribe the interventions at the appropriate intensity to achieve best results. There is good
245 evidence for proprioceptive training, TENS and cryotherapy to improve somatosensory function.
246 However, there is a lack of evidence examining whether these interventions reduce reliance on the
247 visual-motor system. Increasing the complexity of proprioceptive training across type of task,
15
248 amount of visual information, cognitive loading and perturbations may help to improve the
249 effectiveness of proprioceptive training in reducing visual-motor reliance.
250 Key Points
251 Findings: To improve sensorimotor function following ACL injury, clinicians could aim to (1) improve
252 peripheral and central efferent function and (2) improve somatosensory function and reduce
253 reliance on the visual-motor system. Interventions can be implemented early in rehabilitation and
254 progressed over time.
255 Implications: Clinicians can use strength training, NMES and surface EMG biofeedback to improve
256 local and central efferent function. Improving somatosensory function can be achieved through
257 proprioceptive training, TENS and cryotherapy.
258 Caution: There is a lack of prospective research to identify if proprioceptive training can reduce
259 visual-motor reliance.
16

13	                                      Serial Ultrasonography for the
14	                                      Assessment of Healing of Lower Extremity
15	                                      Bone Stress Injury and Correlation With
16	                                      Return to Sport/Exercise
17	                                      Brett G. Toresdahl, MD,†* Justin Conway, MD,‡ Theodore T. Miller, MD,§
18	                                      Marci A. Goolsby, MD,|| Christian S. Geannette, MD,§ Brianna Quijano, MS,¶
19	                                      and Lisa R. Callahan, MD||
20	
21	
22	                                      Background: Lower extremity bone stress injuries (BSIs) are common among athletes who participate in high-impact
23	                                      activities. Conventional imaging is limited in assessing healing of BSIs.
24	                                      Hypothesis: Serial ultrasonography (US) can identify changes in appearance of lower extremity BSIs over time that can be
25	                                      correlated with symptoms and return to exercise/sport.
26	                                      Study Design: Cohort observational study.
27	                                      Level of Evidence: Level 3.
28	                                      Methods: Adults 18 to 50 years old with a recent exercise-associated BSI of distal tibia/fibula or metatarsals diagnosed
29	                                      by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were enrolled. US was performed every 2 weeks for 12 weeks. The sonographic
30	                                      appearance (soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction, hyperemia on power Doppler, callus) was correlated with the numerical
31	                                      rating scale (NRS) for pain and ability to return to sport/exercise.
32	                                      Results: A total of 30 patients were enrolled (mean age, 35.3 ± 7.7 years; 21 [70.0%] female). The tibia was most frequently
33	                                      affected (n = 15, 50.0%), followed by metatarsals (n = 14, 46.7%) and fibula (n = 1, 3.3%). At week 4, 25 of 30 (83.3%) had
34	                                      at least 1 US finding associated with the BSI. The degree of hyperemia was correlated with NRS at weeks 4 and 6 (Spearman
35	                                      correlations [ρ] 0.45 [0.09, 0.69] and 0.42 [0.07, 0.67], respectively), as well as return to sport/exercise at week 6 (ρ -0.45
36	                                      [-0.68, -0.09]). US soft tissue edema was also correlated with NRS at week 6 (ρ 0.38 [0.02, 0.65]).
37	                                      Conclusion: Serial US of lower extremity BSIs can provide objective measures of healing. US findings were correlated with
38	                                      clinical outcomes at multiple timepoints.
39	                                      Clinical Relevance: US may have advantages over conventional imaging for monitoring healing of lower extremity BSIs.
40	                                      Further research is needed to better understand the prognostic value of these sonographic indicators of BSI healing and role
41	                                      in assessing readiness for return to sport/exercise.
42	                                      Keywords: bone stress injury; magnetic resonance imaging; return to play; ultrasonography

                                      Serial Ultrasonography for the
                                      Assessment of Healing of Lower Extremity
                                      Bone Stress Injury and Correlation With
                                      Return to Sport/Exercise
                                      Brett G. Toresdahl, MD,†* Justin Conway, MD,‡ Theodore T. Miller, MD,§
                                      Marci A. Goolsby, MD,|| Christian S. Geannette, MD,§ Brianna Quijano, MS,¶
                                      and Lisa R. Callahan, MD||


                                      Background: Lower extremity bone stress injuries (BSIs) are common among athletes who participate in high-impact
                                      activities. Conventional imaging is limited in assessing healing of BSIs.
                                      Hypothesis: Serial ultrasonography (US) can identify changes in appearance of lower extremity BSIs over time that can be
                                      correlated with symptoms and return to exercise/sport.
                                      Study Design: Cohort observational study.
                                      Level of Evidence: Level 3.
                                      Methods: Adults 18 to 50 years old with a recent exercise-associated BSI of distal tibia/fibula or metatarsals diagnosed
                                      by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were enrolled. US was performed every 2 weeks for 12 weeks. The sonographic
                                      appearance (soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction, hyperemia on power Doppler, callus) was correlated with the numerical
                                      rating scale (NRS) for pain and ability to return to sport/exercise.
                                      Results: A total of 30 patients were enrolled (mean age, 35.3 ± 7.7 years; 21 [70.0%] female). The tibia was most frequently
                                      affected (n = 15, 50.0%), followed by metatarsals (n = 14, 46.7%) and fibula (n = 1, 3.3%). At week 4, 25 of 30 (83.3%) had
                                      at least 1 US finding associated with the BSI. The degree of hyperemia was correlated with NRS at weeks 4 and 6 (Spearman
                                      correlations [ρ] 0.45 [0.09, 0.69] and 0.42 [0.07, 0.67], respectively), as well as return to sport/exercise at week 6 (ρ -0.45
                                      [-0.68, -0.09]). US soft tissue edema was also correlated with NRS at week 6 (ρ 0.38 [0.02, 0.65]).
                                      Conclusion: Serial US of lower extremity BSIs can provide objective measures of healing. US findings were correlated with
                                      clinical outcomes at multiple timepoints.
                                      Clinical Relevance: US may have advantages over conventional imaging for monitoring healing of lower extremity BSIs.
                                      Further research is needed to better understand the prognostic value of these sonographic indicators of BSI healing and role
                                      in assessing readiness for return to sport/exercise.
                                      Keywords: bone stress injury; magnetic resonance imaging; return to play; ultrasonography
