 "id":"Q33",
 "sourceFile":"Secondary injury prevention reduces hamstring strain and time-loss groin injury burdens in male professional football.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Secondary injury prevention reduces hamstring strain and time-loss groin injury burdens in male professional football' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Prospective cohort study over five seasons at one Australian male professional football club, with 73 players in total (39 in the two-season control period and 51 in the three-season intervention period). Post-match isometric knee flexion and hip adduction strength was monitored, and indicated interventions followed strength drops beyond the test's minimal detectable change. Compared with the control period, hamstring strain injury (HSI) burden fell from 25.18 to 20.20 days absence per 1000 h, while HSI incidence was similar (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.33).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The comparison is non-randomised and uses a preceding control period at one club, with 21 to 31 players per season, coaching and medical staff changes, and COVID-19 disruption during the intervention. The burden 95% CIs overlap, and HSI incidence rose non-significantly, so the change cannot be cleanly attributed to the system.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the burden fall as proof that the strength-screening system reduces hamstring and groin injury, when it is a preliminary, non-randomised before-and-after comparison that the authors do not recommend using in isolation.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Adams SR, Wollin M, Drew MK, Toohey LA, Smith C, Borges N, et al. Secondary injury prevention reduces hamstring strain and time-loss groin injury burdens in male professional football. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.ptsp.2024.08.003",
   "abstract":"Prospective cohort study of 73 male professional football players at one Australian club over five seasons: two control seasons with usual care, then three intervention seasons with a systems-based secondary injury prevention system using post-match isometric knee flexion and hip adduction strength testing. Burdens were compared between periods. HSI burden fell by 4.98 days absence per 1000 h (19.8%) and time-loss groin burden by 3.93 days absence per 1000 h (25.6%) in the intervention period.",
   "tldr":"At one professional club, adding post-match strength screening with indicated responses was followed by lower hamstring strain and groin injury burdens than the two previous seasons. The design is a non-randomised comparison with earlier seasons, so this is a preliminary signal rather than proof of effect.",
   "methods":"Prospective cohort over five seasons (2016/17 to 2020/21) at one male professional club. The first two seasons were usual care; the next three added testing two days post-match of unilateral knee flexion and side-lying hip adduction maximum voluntary isometric contractions. An alert was raised when a player's strength fell beyond the test's minimal detectable change from their 8-test moving average, and a retest the next day guided physiotherapy, strengthening and load reductions. Incidence rates were compared with Poisson-type regression, and burden (days absence per 1000 player hours) was reported with 95% CIs without a significance test.",
   "findings":"HSI burden was 20.20 versus 25.18 days absence per 1000 h (4.98 lower, 19.8%), with match HSI burden down 59.0%; HSI incidence was similar (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.33, p = 0.93). Time-loss groin burden was 11.44 versus 15.37 days per 1000 h (3.93 lower, 25.6%), and groin incidence was lower (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.34, p = 0.17), which was not significant. The intervention period produced 30 strength-reduction alerts for 17 players.",
   "limitations":"Non-randomised, with a historical control period and a single club. The abstract reports the groin change as 0.57 days absence per 1000 h (49.1%), but the Results give the burden change as 3.93 days per 1000 h (25.6%); the 49% figure is the drop in incidence (1.16 to 0.59 per 1000 h). Burden differences were not tested statistically and their CIs overlap, and groin injury severity rose (13 to 19 days per injury, p = 0.167) even as burden fell. The authors note a possible lead-time effect and possible staff influence on return-to-play decisions.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clubs with a sports-medicine-led process could consider regular post-match isometric strength testing with pre-set alerts, followed by individual load and position-based changes, alongside usual primary and tertiary prevention. The authors advise against using this testing in isolation.",
   "athleteDev":"Post-match isometric knee flexion and hip adduction testing, with alerts set against each player's own recent average, can guide training exposure for players whose strength has dropped. Dominant limbs and forwards and wide players were more often flagged in this study.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It did not test return-to-play criteria or outcomes, and the authors note that the boundary between end of time loss and return to play is not objectively clear."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "paper.methods: said burden was compared with Poisson-type models -> Poisson regression applied to incidence; burden reported descriptively with CIs ('Poisson regression was used to analyse injury incidence rates'; Table 1 burden p values '-')",
     "paper.limitations: 'Only the HSI and groin differences in incidence were tested' -> burden not tested; added that groin severity rose ('19 ± 8 days lost' vs '13 ± 8', p = 0.167)",
     "synthesisCaution and tldr: 'uncontrolled' -> non-randomised comparison with a preceding control period ('compared with those from an immediately preceding two-season control period')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Journal pre-proof; volume and pages not printed, so citation has year only.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q34",
 "sourceFile":"Selecting Metrics That Matter - Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and I.pdf",
 "decision":"DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"The article's own DOI is not printed in the text; the only DOI-like strings are reference-list items or none. All other fields are filled and doiMissing is true, so the operator can verify the DOI externally.",
 "doiMissing":true,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Selecting Metrics That Matter: Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing' matches the filename, which is truncated at 'and I'.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of how the countermovement jump (CMJ) is used for performance profiling, neuromuscular fatigue monitoring and rehabilitation testing, drawing on published correlation and fatigue studies. It reports that jump height and peak power correlate with strength, linear speed and change of direction, but that jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (ES -0.04 each) in a meta-analysis of 151 studies, while other cited studies found time-based metrics changed more. Worked examples use hypothetical data for 20 athletes and 3 individuals.",
 "screeningLimitations":"No systematic search is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked, and the correlations quoted come from varied populations and tests. The worked examples use hypothetical data, and the article's own DOI is not printed in the text.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the list of metrics in Figure 1 as validated for their own squad, when the article offers it as a reasoned framework supported by a narrative literature summary and anecdotal experience.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Bishop C, Jordan M, Torres-Ronda L, Loturco I, Harry J, Virgile A, et al. Selecting Metrics That Matter: Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2023.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"The countermovement jump (CMJ) is one of the most used performance assessments in strength and conditioning. The article discusses how the metrics selected from CMJ testing may differ when the test is used as a proxy for athletic performance, as part of neuromuscular fatigue monitoring, or as part of a test battery for return to performance in injured athletes.",
   "tldr":"The metrics worth tracking from a countermovement jump depend on why the test is being used. Jump height and peak power track strength and speed well but respond poorly to fatigue, so time-based metrics are often more useful for fatigue monitoring.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published CMJ studies on associations with strength, speed and change of direction, fatigue sensitivity and injury rehabilitation, with a proposed framework (Figure 1) for metric selection. No systematic search is described. Worked examples use hypothetical group and individual data to show how the coefficient of variation can set the threshold for real change.",
   "findings":"Jump height and peak power were consistently associated with strength, linear speed and change of direction in the cited studies. In a meta-analysis of 151 fatigue studies (63 CMJ metrics), maximal jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (ES -0.04 each); in other cited studies, relative net impulse and flight time changed most immediately after intense exercise, and time to peak power and flight time:contraction time ratio changed most over 24 to 72 hours. In a cited snowboard cross study, acute fatigue reduced absolute peak force (ES -2.15) and increased the time measures. Worked example: a 2.9% change in jump height was smaller than the 3.8% CV, so it cannot be called real, while a 6.2% change in time to take-off was larger than its 4.2% CV.",
   "limitations":"The review does not describe how studies were searched or selected, and it relies on the authors' anecdotal experience for parts of the framework. Many correlations are drawn from different populations and tests, and the worked examples are explicitly hypothetical. The article focuses on kinetic data from a force plate and does not weigh video or kinematic measures. The article's own DOI is not printed in the text.",
   "practicalImplications":"Choose CMJ metrics according to the purpose of testing: outcome metrics such as jump height, force and power for performance profiling, time-based metrics and RSI-modified for fatigue monitoring, and landing force and inter-limb asymmetry for rehabilitation. Before reading a change as real, compare it with the metric's own coefficient of variation, measured by test-retest, using group or individual thresholds.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance profiling, CMJ height, force and power link to strength, sprint and change of direction measures and can be used as proxies. For a squad, check whether a change exceeds each metric's own test-retest variation before acting on it.",
   "rtp":"The article only briefly covers injured athletes and does not validate any return-to-sport threshold. It suggests landing force and asymmetry measures may show residual deficits better than jump height or power, but it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "paper.findings: named time to take-off as a metric that changed over 24 to 72 h -> time to peak power and flight time:contraction time ratio; immediate changes were relative net impulse and flight time ('over subsequent days (e.g., 24-72 hours), metrics such as time to peak power ... and flight time:contraction time ratio')",
     "evidenceSummary: implied the 151-study meta-analysis showed time-based metrics changed more -> attributed to other cited studies ('In contrast, previous studies have shown that some time-based metrics')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Own DOI not printed; header shows 'VOLUME 00 | NUMBER 00 | MONTH 2023', so the 2023 year comes from an online-first header and volume/issue are omitted.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

input.content:
{
 "id":"Q36",
 "sourceFile":"Sensitivity and specificity of on-field visible signs of concussion in the National Football League.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Sensitivity and Specificity of On-Field Visible Signs of Concussion in the National Football League' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Brain Health & Psychology","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional video review of 251 NFL injury plays from the 2017 season, 211 with a diagnosed sport-related concussion (SRC) and 40 without, scored independently by two expert raters using an AFL visible-signs checklist. Slow to get up was the most frequent sign in concussed players (65.9% averaged across raters), and about 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. The checklist as a whole had sensitivity of 73% and specificity of 65% (AUC 0.66, which the authors classify as poor), and motor incoordination and loss of responsiveness were the only signs that remained significant in multivariate analysis.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only two raters, one season, and players removed from play for suspected concussion were included, so the findings may not generalise to other levels or to all head impacts. The comparison group was only 40 non-concussed plays, the multivariate odds ratios have wide CIs (loss of responsiveness 1.14 to 23.42), and the authors state that visible signs alone are inadequate for diagnosis.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read a high-specificity sign, such as motor incoordination or loss of responsiveness, as enough to diagnose concussion, when the authors state that the diagnosis cannot be made from visible signs alone and that a multimodal sideline evaluation is required.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Elbin RJ, Zuckerman SL, Sills AK, Crandall JR, Lessley DJ, Solomon GS. Sensitivity and Specificity of On-Field Visible Signs of Concussion in the National Football League. Neurosurgery. 2020.",
   "doi":"10.1093/neuros/nyaa072",
   "abstract":"Video review by two expert raters of 251 NFL injury plays from the 2017 season (211 diagnosed with sport-related concussion, 40 not) using a visible-signs checklist. Slow to get up and motor incoordination were the most frequent signs in concussed players, slow to get up was the most sensitive, and 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. The checklist had sensitivity of 73%, specificity of 65% and an AUC of 0.66, which the authors call poor, so concussion cannot be diagnosed from visible signs alone.",
   "tldr":"In NFL video review, the visible-signs checklist missed about a quarter of diagnosed concussions and had poor overall discrimination (AUC 0.66). Visible signs are one part of the sideline evaluation, not a diagnostic tool on their own.",
   "methods":"Prospective observational cross-sectional study using video of injury plays from the 2017 NFL season where a player was removed for suspected concussion. Two expert raters independently scored the AFL visible-signs checklist for each play. Logistic regression tested each sign, and a receiver operating characteristic curve with AUC summarised the checklist. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated against the team physician and neurotrauma consultant's diagnosis.",
   "findings":"Concussed players most often showed slow to get up (averaged 65.9%) and motor incoordination (28.4%). In non-concussed players, slow to get up was also most common (60.0%). The checklist had combined sensitivity of 73.46% and specificity of 65.0%, and 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. Multivariate logistic regression identified motor incoordination (OR 3.96, 95% CI 1.64 to 9.56, P = .002) and loss of responsiveness (OR 5.17, 95% CI 1.14 to 23.42, P = .033) as significant predictors. The AUC was 0.66.",
   "limitations":"Two raters, with no third rater to resolve disagreements; only one season; only players removed for suspected concussion were reviewed; and a league-specific checklist. The Discussion states sensitivity and specificity of 76% and 63%, but the Results and Table 5 give 73% and 65% combined, so the Discussion figures should not be quoted. The sign definitions differ from the new consensus list, and several authors are employed by or consult for the NFL.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use visible-sign checks as one input to a full sideline or acute evaluation, not as a stand-alone screen.  "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 1): What Is It? How Can Clinicians Assess It?' matches the filename.",

 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Injured Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Clinical commentary that works as a narrative clinical review, with no described search method, summarising evidence on sensorimotor changes after ACL injury and proposing clinic-based tests. The authors describe dysfunction across afferent pathways (pain, swelling, reduced proprioception, increased visual-motor reliance and cortical processing) and efferent pathways (reduced motor cortex and corticospinal excitability, spinal reflex excitability reduced acutely then increased chronically). They recommend joint position sense, pain, effusion, visual-motor reliance and processing, strength and surface EMG activation tests.",
 "screeningLimitations":"No search or selection method is described, and several recommendations, retest intervals and the stepdown visual-reliance test rest on the authors' clinical practice and unpublished reliability data. The article reports no new study and does not link any test to reinjury.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the proposed test battery and its retest intervals as a validated reinjury screen, when the authors state that visual-motor tests still need normative values and research on whether they relate to reinjury.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Vitharana TN, King E, Welch N, Devitt B, Moran K. Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 1): What Is It? How Can Clinicians Assess It? Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.2519/jospt.2025.12725",
   "abstract":"Clinical commentary asking what sensorimotor dysfunction follows ACL injury and how clinicians can assess it. Dysfunction is described across afferent pathways (pain and swelling, increased central processing, reduced proprioception, increased visual-motor reliance) and efferent pathways (reduced cortical and descending motor excitability, spinal reflex excitability acutely reduced then chronically increased). The authors propose practical tests of proprioception, pain, swelling, visual-motor reliance and processing, strength and voluntary activation.",
   "tldr":"Sensorimotor dysfunction after ACL injury spans pain, swelling, proprioception, visual reliance and quadriceps activation, and most of it can be screened with simple clinic tests. The battery is expert-proposed and has not been validated against reinjury.",
   "methods":"Narrative clinical commentary by five authors from sports medicine and university settings. The authors summarise mechanistic and clinical studies by subsystem (somatosensory, visual, efferent) and tabulate clinical tests with their equipment, facilitators and barriers. No literature search or appraisal method is described.",
   "findings":"The authors cite knee proprioception deficits after ACLR compared with both the uninjured limb and healthy controls, including a joint position error of 7.2 degrees in the ACLR limb versus 1.9 degrees in the uninjured limb in 10 elite athletes. They cite increased visual cortex activity after ACLR and quadriceps voluntary activation deficits up to four years after surgery. For their own adapted stepdown test they report ICCs of 0.71 to 0.96 (unpublished) and that healthy athletes improved time to stability by 17% with eyes closed.",
   "limitations":"No search or appraisal method, and the authors describe their recommendations as driven by clinical practice. The stepdown reliability and healthy-athlete data are unpublished, the suggested retest intervals (joint position sense every 4 to 6 weeks, strength every 6 to 8 weeks, EMG every 2 weeks) are practice-based, and the neurocognitive and sensory-station tests have no reliability data in ACLR patients. Most numbers quoted come from cited studies, not from new data.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians can track pain (VAS or NRS) and effusion (sweep or ballottement test) each session, joint position sense with an image-based method, quadriceps and hamstring strength by isokinetic or handheld dynamometry, and between-limb quadriceps activation with surface EMG. The authors cite isokinetic peak torque values for elite field-based athletes (quadriceps and hamstrings 3.19 and 1.78 Nm/kg in males, 2.32 and 1.36 Nm/kg in females) and a between-limb EMG difference above 22% to 30% as possibly clinically relevant.",
   "athleteDev":"The cited strength values for elite field-based athletes can help frame late-stage strength targets after ACL injury. The article does not test whether reaching these values improves performance.",
   "rtp":"The paper informs which sensorimotor domains to assess during ACL rehabilitation but proposes no return-to-sport criteria or cut-offs, and the visual-motor tests have no normative values or link to reinjury yet. It cannot be used as a clearance test battery."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"DECISION_CHANGED",
   "changes":[
     "decision: EXCLUDE (b) commentary -> INCLUDE as Narrative Review. The article is a structured clinical review of evidence (Background, Clinical question, Key results, Clinical application, three evidence tables, Key Points, about 105 references); 'no search method described' defines a Narrative Review, which INSTRUCTIONS lists as eligible, not an exclusion ('This clinical commentary outlines sensorimotor changes ... and proposes evidence-based methods')",

     "paper.doi: set to 10.2519/jospt.2025.12725 from the article header ('https://doi.org/10.2519/https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2025.12725')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"The article labels itself a 'clinical commentary'; a reviewer may decide that JOSPT clinical commentaries fall under exclusion (b) instead.    "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

 "sourceFile":"Serial ultrasonography for the assessment of healing of lower extremity bone stress injury and correlation with return to sport.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Serial Ultrasonography for the Assessment of Healing of Lower Extremity Bone Stress Injury and Correlation With Return to Sport/Exercise' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Endurance Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Prospective observational cohort of adults aged 18 to 50 with an exercise-related lower-leg or metatarsal bone stress injury confirmed by MRI, followed with ultrasound every two weeks for 12 weeks; 30 patients were analysed (mean age 35.3 years, 70% female, 90% running-related). Soft tissue edema and power Doppler hyperemia fell significantly over 12 weeks, and hyperemia correlated with pain at weeks 4 and 6 (rho 0.45 and 0.42) and with lower return-to-sport ratings at week 6 (rho -0.45). Persistent marrow edema on MRI at 12 weeks did not correlate with pain or return to sport.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Single-centre, uncontrolled cohort with 30 analysed patients, a subjective 0 to 3 ultrasound grading, and a non-validated return-to-sport Likert scale. Most correlations are weak (none above 0.5), and only a few time points were significant, so the study cannot show that ultrasound predicts return to sport.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the correlations as proof that ultrasound findings can time a return to sport, when the authors describe them as preliminary and call for research on their prognostic value.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Toresdahl BG, Conway J, Miller TT, Goolsby MA, Geannette CS, Quijano B, et al. Serial Ultrasonography for the Assessment of Healing of Lower Extremity Bone Stress Injury and Correlation With Return to Sport/Exercise. Sports Health. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1177/19417381241231590",
   "abstract":"Prospective observational cohort of adults aged 18 to 50 with an MRI-confirmed exercise-related bone stress injury of the distal tibia, fibula or metatarsals. Serial ultrasound every two weeks for 12 weeks was correlated with pain (NRS) and return-to-sport ratings. Soft tissue edema and hyperemia decreased over time; hyperemia correlated with pain at weeks 4 and 6 and with return to sport at week 6.",
   "tldr":"Ultrasound of lower-leg and foot stress injuries showed edema and hyperemia fading over 12 weeks, and hyperemia tracked pain and return-to-sport ratings around weeks 4 to 6. The correlations are weak and the study is small, so ultrasound looks promising for monitoring but is not a return-to-sport test yet.",
   "methods":"Adults aged 18 to 50 with a recent exercise-related distal tibia, fibula or metatarsal bone stress injury confirmed by MRI were enrolled within four weeks of MRI and scanned every two weeks for 12 weeks. Two blinded musculoskeletal radiologists scored soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction, hyperemia (0 to 3) and callus. Patients completed pain (NRS) and return-to-sport surveys biweekly, and MRI was repeated at 12 weeks. Repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t tests and Spearman correlations were used.",
   "findings":"Of 31 enrolled, 30 were analysed. Soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction and hyperemia were seen on ultrasound at some point in 66.7%, 63.3% and 43.3% of patients. Soft tissue edema fell from 0.95 at week 2 to 0.34 at week 12 and hyperemia from 0.63 to 0.07 (both P < .01); periosteal reaction did not change significantly in Table 3 (P = .23). Hyperemia correlated with average pain at week 4 (rho 0.45, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.69) and week 6 (rho 0.42, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.67), and with return to sport at week 6 (rho -0.45, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.09); patients with hyperemia at week 6 had higher pain in later weeks (P = .04) but not clearly lower return-to-sport ratings (P = .06). Soft tissue edema correlated with pain at week 6 (rho 0.38). MRI marrow edema fell from 1.3 to 0.79 (P < .01), but it persisted in 53.3% at 12 weeks and did not correlate with pain or return to sport.",
   "limitations":"Single centre, no comparison group, small sample, and a 4-point subjective ultrasound scale with inter-observer variability. The return-to-sport scale was not validated, most patients had not fully returned by week 12, and no ultrasound correlations with clinical outcomes were significant after week 6. The Results text says periosteal reaction decreased significantly (all P < .01), but Table 3 gives P = .23; the abstract says 30 patients were enrolled, but the Results say 31 were enrolled and one was excluded after week 2; and Table 1 gives metatarsal 49.7% while the text gives 46.7%.",
   "practicalImplications":"Ultrasound every two weeks could track hyperemia and soft tissue edema alongside symptoms, which may help where repeat MRI is less useful. The authors note athletic training rooms may be able to use it, but the findings support clinical judgment rather than replacing it.",
   "athleteDev":"Not a performance application. Staff who manage progression after a bone stress injury could look at the trend in hyperemia and symptoms, but the study does not test load or training decisions.",
   "rtp":"Hyperemia at week 6 was associated with lower return-to-sport ratings, so it may be a useful added signal. The paper cannot set a clearance threshold: correlations were weak, the return-to-sport scale was not validated, and no prognostic cut-off was derived."
 },

   "status":"CORRECTED",

{
 "id":"Q40",
 "sourceFile":"Serial ultrasound imaging leading up to an Achilles tendon rupture after identification of a thickened paratenon.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Serial Ultrasound Imaging Leading up to an Achilles Tendon Rupture After Identification of a Thickened Paratenon: A Case Report' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Case Report / Case Series",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Injured Athletes","Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Case report of one 22-year-old male collegiate lacrosse midfielder. Ultrasound seven months before injury showed normal Achilles tendons, and about two weeks before rupture repeat ultrasound showed a normal-appearing tendon with new hypoechoic paratenon thickening 1 to 4 cm proximal to the calcaneus. A complete midsubstance Achilles rupture occurred on push-off, and MRI two days later confirmed a complete rupture with severe tendinosis of the distal remnant, while the paratenon was intact at surgery.",
 "screeningLimitations":"A single athlete with ultrasound at only two time points before rupture and no histopathology, so the timeline of paratenon change cannot be established. The athlete had started new cleats, was taking meloxicam prescribed by the team physician and was doing an eccentric rehabilitation program, any of which could affect the course, and the case cannot show whether paratenon thickening causes or predicts rupture.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat paratenon thickening on ultrasound as a warning sign that predicts rupture, when this is one case and the authors say the paratenon's role in rupture remains unclear and the thickening may be a normal healing response.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Ford K, Monson N, Glauser S, Cushman DM. Serial Ultrasound Imaging Leading up to an Achilles Tendon Rupture After Identification of a Thickened Paratenon: A Case Report. American Journal of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation. 2025;104(11):1067-1069.",
   "doi":"10.1097/PHM.0000000000002826",
   "abstract":"A 22-year-old collegiate lacrosse student-athlete had normal Achilles tendons on ultrasound seven months before injury. About four weeks before rupture he developed pain, and repeat ultrasound showed a normal-appearing tendon with new hypoechoic paratenon thickening. He then suffered a complete Achilles rupture. The case is the second known rupture preceded by normal asymptomatic advanced imaging and raises questions about the paratenon's role in rupture.",
   "tldr":"A collegiate lacrosse player with a normal Achilles on ultrasound seven months earlier developed new paratenon thickening about two weeks before a complete rupture. One case cannot show whether paratenon thickening predicts rupture, but the authors suggest extra caution when it is seen acutely in explosive athletes.",
   "methods":"Single case report following CARE guidelines. The athlete had a research ultrasound of both Achilles tendons seven months before injury, and symptomatic pain prompted a clinical exam and repeat ultrasound about two weeks before rupture. MRI was performed two days after rupture, and surgery was undertaken five days after injury.",
   "findings":"At the initial scan, both tendons were normal. Repeat ultrasound about two weeks before rupture showed a normal-appearing tendon with hypoechoic paratenon thickening on the medial superficial surface, 1 to 4 cm above the calcaneus, while the plantaris was intact. The rupture occurred during push-off. MRI showed a complete rupture and severe tendinosis of the remnant distal tendon, which ultrasound had not shown two weeks earlier. The paratenon was not ruptured at surgery.",
   "limitations":"One athlete and one case, with only two ultrasound time points before rupture and no histopathology of the tendon or paratenon. Meloxicam was prescribed and new cleats had been introduced, so the paratenon change cannot be attributed to a single cause. The authors note the thickening may have been a normal healing response.",
   "practicalImplications":"Acute paratenon thickening on ultrasound in an athlete with Achilles pain may merit closer follow-up, especially in explosive sports, as the authors suggest. The case does not set a threshold for restricting training or for predicting rupture.",
   "athleteDev":"Not a performance application. The case links new cleats and conditioning to the onset of pain, but the paper does not establish a cause, so staff should not treat footwear changes as a proven risk.",
   "rtp":"The paper gives no return-to-play timeline or criteria; the athlete returned gradually after open repair under a standard protocol. It does not show whether paratenon findings should change return timing, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play decisions."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "screeningLimitations: 'The authors also prescribed meloxicam and changed cleats' -> the athlete had started new cleats and took meloxicam prescribed by the team physician, alongside an eccentric program ('in the context of using new cleats during conditioning'; 'took meloxicam as prescribed by the team physician')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Single case; mentions NSAID (meloxicam) use before rupture, and the authors note it is unknown how NSAIDs affect paratenon healing.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}
